senses.definition: Splitting a model itself across several devices because it is too large for one.

core.definition: A technique for splitting a single large model across several devices, such as GPUs, because it is too big to fit on one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAIR in 'parallelism', with a secondary stress on the first word. The 'al' in 'parallel' is a reduced vowel and the word ends in '-lel-iz-um', not '-lay-lism'. The middle 'l' is a clear l, and the final syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: neutral, a technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers training large language models use this term in design reviews and technical documentation. It usually appears alongside 'data parallelism' and 'pipeline parallelism' in discussions of distributed training. In casual talk, people might say 'splitting the model across GPUs' instead.

distinctions.note: Data parallelism copies the whole model to each device and splits the training data, while model parallelism splits the model itself.
Pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive layers to different devices and passes data through them in stages, which is one form of model parallelism.

collocations: combine model parallelism with data parallelism

examples.everyday: My friend who trains AI models said they had to use model parallelism because the model was too big to fit on one graphics card.
examples.professional: We will use model parallelism across eight GPUs, but the communication overhead will slow each training step unless we tune the batch size.
examples.analytical: Model parallelism trades memory constraints for communication costs, so its scalability depends on how the network architecture partitions its computations.

nuance.analogy: It is like splitting a large orchestra score so each section plays its own part on a different stage, then coordinating the timing between them.
nuance.etymology: 'Model' comes from Latin modulus, a measure; 'parallel' comes from Greek parallēlos, alongside one another.
common_mistakes: Confusing model parallelism with data parallelism; the first splits the model, the second splits the data.
Stressing the wrong syllable in 'parallelism'; the main stress is on PAIR, not the final syllable.

conversation.text: Model parallelism splits the model itself across devices when it's too big for one.
Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism are both forms of model parallelism.
Model parallelism adds communication overhead, so we use it only for the biggest models.

senses.definition: Of or relating to monergism.

core.definition: Describing a view of salvation in which God alone, without human cooperation, produces regeneration and faith in a person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'jis,' the third syllable. The first syllables have weak 'er' sounds, so don't stress 'MAH' or add extra vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theological discussion. It describes a position, so the tone depends on whether the speaker agrees with it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monergistic almost exclusively in theology and seminary contexts. It usually modifies words like 'view,' 'regeneration,' or 'doctrine.' In everyday talk, people simply say that God alone does the saving work.

distinctions.note: Synergistic describes a view where God and humans cooperate, while monergistic describes a view where God alone acts.
Calvinistic is broader and describes a whole theological system, while monergistic is specific to the role of God in regeneration.

examples.everyday: My pastor's sermon was really monergistic, saying that God does the whole work of salvation.
examples.professional: The monergistic framing of the document helped the committee explain why our grace-based policies had no conditions.
examples.analytical: A monergistic account of regeneration takes the Holy Spirit's action as the sole cause of the new birth, which raises difficult questions about human responsibility.

nuance.analogy: A monergistic view is like a painter who creates the whole painting alone, with the canvas merely receiving the paint.
nuance.etymology: From monergism plus the suffix -istic, from Greek monos 'alone' and ergon 'work.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the third (MAH-ner-JIS-tik).
Using monergistic as a general word for 'only one person doing something' outside theology.

senses.definition: A patch which alters the behavior of a program by forcibly overriding aspects of the original code at runtime.
To alter the behavior of a program by forcibly overriding aspects of the original code at runtime.

core.definition: A change that alters a program's behavior at runtime by overriding parts of its original code, without editing the source.

pronunciation.tip: Give MUNG-kee secondary stress and PACH primary stress. The word monkey is usually reduced to MUNG-ki in fast speech, and the ng is a single sound with no hard g.

nuance.connotation: mixed: programmers use it casually, but it can imply a quick, fragile fix.
nuance.usage_note: American developers use monkey patch in code reviews, Slack and documentation. It is informal and often carries a hint of risk, so teams may say 'we monkey patched it' to admit a temporary workaround. It is not a term outsiders usually need.

distinctions.note: A hotfix is an official, tested emergency release; a monkey patch is a runtime change that may bypass normal review.
Refactoring restructures code cleanly without changing behavior; a monkey patch overrides code from outside.

examples.everyday: My phone app kept crashing, so the developer said they'd monkey patch it until the update.
examples.professional: We can't wait for the vendor release, so let's monkey patch the library in staging and open a ticket.
examples.analytical: Monkey patching offers flexibility in dynamic languages, but it makes program behavior depend on load order and hides dependencies.

nuance.analogy: Like taping a cable over a broken part of a machine, a monkey patch works now but may cause trouble later.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word in formal documents; use monkey patch or monkey-patch.
Using it for any bug fix; it specifically means overriding code at runtime.

monkey-patch.etymology: Apparently from earlier *guerrilla patch* (“code that sneakily changes other code”), understood as gorilla patch.

senses.definition: Containing holes by having been eaten by moth larvae.
Old and in poor condition; worn-out.
Antiquated; having been in use a long time.

core.definition: Full of holes because moth larvae have eaten the fabric, or old, worn out, and in poor condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first word, MOTH, and then on the second part of the phrase, EE, with the final syllable reduced to a weak 'uhn'. Non-native speakers often stress the wrong syllable or pronounce the 'th' as a 't'.

nuance.connotation: negative, suggesting something shabby, outdated, or falling apart.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say moth-eaten for old clothes, blankets, or a worn-out couch, and sometimes for an outdated idea or old policy. It is informal and vivid, so it can sound a bit harsh if used about a person's feelings or a friend's sweater. It is common in casual description and in writing that wants a sharp image.

distinctions.note: Worn out is a general term for used up, while moth-eaten specifically suggests holes and decay.
Outdated is neutral about condition, while moth-eaten adds the image of something shabby and falling apart.

examples.everyday: Grandma finally threw out her moth-eaten wool blanket after forty years.
examples.professional: The old reporting dashboard looks moth-eaten, so we should rebuild it before the audit.
examples.analytical: The author dismisses the moth-eaten doctrines of his predecessors as relics that no longer serve the argument.

nuance.analogy: Moth-eaten is like a sweater with lace-like holes: once solid, now riddled with gaps.
nuance.etymology: Compound of moth and eaten, from Old English etan, to eat.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen when writing it.
Stressing MOTH-eaten as one unit without the reduced final syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Moth-eaten is not a biblical phrase, but the image appears in Scripture. James 5:2 (RSV) says riches have rotted and garments are moth-eaten, a warning against hoarding wealth. The phrase illustrates how worldly possessions decay.

senses.definition: Anything that mutes or deadens sound.
A warm piece of clothing for the hands.
A kiln or furnace, often electric, with no direct flames (a muffle furnace)
The bare end of the nose between the nostrils, especially in ruminants.
A machine with two pulleys to hoist load by spinning wheels, polyspast, block and tackle.
To wrap (a person, face etc.) in fabric or another covering, for warmth or protection; often with up.
To wrap up or cover (a source of noise) in order to deaden the sound.
senses.example: to muffle the strings of a drum, or that part of an oar which rests in the rowlock

senses.definition: To mute or deaden (a sound etc.).
To speak indistinctly, or without clear articulation.
To prevent seeing, or hearing, or speaking, by wraps bound about the head; to blindfold; to deafen.

core.definition: To make a sound quieter or less clear, or to wrap something to reduce noise or protect it from cold.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a syllabic l with no separate vowel. The word is two syllables, not 'muf-fuhl' with a clear vowel in the second.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It describes making sound quieter, and it can be positive when people want quiet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'muffle the sound' or 'muffle the TV' when they want quiet in a house or office. In cold weather, 'muffle up' or 'be muffled up' means to wrap warmly with a scarf and hat. The noun 'muffler' is more common in American English for a car part, so be careful when you hear the word in a car shop.

distinctions.note: Mute can mean to turn off sound completely, while muffle means to reduce or soften it without stopping it.
Dampen usually refers to reducing energy, enthusiasm, or moisture; muffle is specifically about sound or being covered for warmth.

examples.everyday: Can you close the door so the TV noise is muffled a bit while I'm on the phone?
examples.professional: We added foam panels to the conference room so that the conversation was muffled for people in the hallway.
examples.analytical: The author argues that institutional language muffles dissent by making disagreement sound technical rather than moral.

nuance.analogy: Muffling sound is like putting a thick blanket over a ringing alarm clock: you can still hear it, but it is no longer piercing.
nuance.etymology: From Old French mouffler, to cover the face or wrap up.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'muffle' with 'muffler,' which is the car part.
Using 'muffle' for turning sound off completely, which is closer to 'mute.'

muffle.etymology: From Middle English *muflen* (“to muffle”), aphetic alteration of Anglo-Norman *amoufler*, from Old French *enmoufler* (“to wrap up, muffle”), from *moufle* (“mitten”), from Medieval Latin *muffula* (“a muff”), of origin (—first recorded in the Capitulary…

senses.definition: A transcendental union of soul or mind with the divine reality or divinity.
The beliefs, ideas, or thoughts of mystics.
A doctrine of direct communication or spiritual intuition of divine truth.
Obscure thoughts and speculations.

core.definition: The belief or practice of seeking direct experience of, or union with, God or ultimate reality beyond ordinary understanding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a short 'i' as in 'miss'. The middle syllable is reduced to 'tuh', and the ending is 'siz-um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or positive in religious studies; can sound vague, irrational, or suspicious in casual use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for religious traditions and also loosely for anything spiritual or mysterious. Scholars use it more precisely for direct experience of the divine. Among Christians, it can be seen as deeply devotional or as a risky departure from doctrine.

distinctions.note: Spirituality is broader and more common, covering any pursuit of meaning or the sacred.
Occultism deals with hidden or secret powers and practices, not necessarily union with God.
Rationalism relies on reason, while mysticism emphasizes experience beyond reason.

examples.everyday: My grandmother loved reading about mysticism and the lives of the saints.
examples.professional: The seminar on mysticism looks at Meister Eckhart, Teresa of Avila, and Gregory Palamas.
examples.analytical: Orthodox mysticism holds that union with God is participation in divine energies, not absorption into the divine essence.

nuance.analogy: Mysticism is like standing at the edge of the ocean and feeling its depth, rather than reading a map.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mystikos, 'secret, connected with mysteries', from mystes, 'initiate'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel like 'my' instead of 'miss'.
Using it to mean fake or supernatural tricks.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as 'mis-TIS-i-zum'.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not biblical, but many point to experiences such as Paul's being caught up to the third heaven in 2 Corinthians 12:2-4. John 15:4 speaks of abiding in Christ, and 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of sharing the divine nature, a text important to Orthodox ideas of theosis.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy treats mystical experience as part of ordinary church life, rooted in prayer, sacraments, and theosis. Hesychasm and the teaching of Gregory Palamas on divine energies are central.
Catholicism honors mystics such as Teresa of Avila and John of the Cross, within doctrine and under church discernment. Mystical union is seen as a gift of grace, not a human achievement.

Protestants are divided: Luther and Calvin spoke of union with Christ, but many Protestants distrust mysticism that bypasses Scripture. Pietist, Quaker, Pentecostal, and some Reformed traditions give experience of God greater weight.

mysticism.etymology: From *mystic* + *-ism*, from Old French *mistique* (“mysterious, full of mystery”), from Latin *mysticus* (“mystical, mystic, of secret rites”), from Ancient Greek *μυστικός* (“secret, mystic”), from *μύστης* (“one who has been initiated, initiate”) from…

senses.definition: A statement Q in relation to statement P such that P implies Q.

core.definition: A condition Q that must hold whenever a statement P holds; if P is true, Q must also be true, so P implies Q.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DISH in condition, and the word necessary is stressed on its middle syllable -SAIR-, not on the first syllable. The -ary ending reduces to a short ee sound, and the r is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is standard vocabulary in mathematics, logic and statistics, used in lectures, proofs and technical writing. In casual speech Americans would say it only when explaining a logical requirement, such as saying something is a necessary condition for a result.

distinctions.note: A necessary condition must hold for P to hold, but it may not be enough by itself; a sufficient condition guarantees P when it holds.
A necessary and sufficient condition is both required and enough, so it is an if-and-only-if relationship.

collocations: necessary condition for the theorem to hold

examples.everyday: Having a valid ticket is a necessary condition for getting into the concert, but it isn't the only thing you need.
examples.professional: Finite variance is a necessary condition for this estimator to be unbiased, so we should check it before running the model.
examples.analytical: If the argument is valid, then the premises are a necessary condition of the conclusion, since no valid argument can have true premises and a false conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A necessary condition is like oxygen for a fire: without it there is no fire, but oxygen alone does not start one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin necessarius, needful, and condicio, agreement or stipulation.
common_mistakes: Confusing necessary with sufficient, so that a required condition is treated as a guarantee
Stressing necessary on the first syllable as NESS-uh-ser-ee rather than the middle

senses.definition: Sinful, villainous, criminal, or wicked, especially when noteworthy or notorious for such characteristics.
senses.example: Aliens have a nefarious connotation in many science fiction books.

core.definition: Wicked, evil, or criminal, especially in a way that is well known or openly shameful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'fair', and the 'ious' ending is two syllables, 'ee-us', not 'shus'. The first vowel is a short, reduced 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes villainy or criminal intent, often with a slightly dramatic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nefarious' in news, fiction, and everyday talk about schemes or plots, often with a playful or dramatic tone. It is a bit formal, so 'shady' or 'sneaky' is more casual. You can say 'nefarious plan' or 'nefarious scheme' naturally in conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Evil' is a broad moral word, while 'nefarious' focuses on criminal or secretive wickedness.
'Sinister' suggests a threatening or ominous atmosphere, while 'nefarious' emphasizes actual wrongdoing.

examples.everyday: My neighbor thinks the guy across the street is up to something nefarious, but I think he just collects old bikes.
examples.professional: Security flagged a set of nefarious login attempts coming from several unfamiliar IP addresses last night.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of the stolen pear suggests that even small acts can reveal a nefarious will turned away from God.

nuance.analogy: A nefarious plan is like a dark alley in a city: you can tell something bad is hidden there even before you see it clearly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'nefarius', from 'nefas', meaning something unlawful or impious, from 'ne-' (not) and 'fas' (divine law).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (NEF-air-ee-us) instead of the second.
Saying 'nefarious' for a merely unpleasant or bad situation; it implies deliberate wrongdoing.

nefarious.etymology: From Latin *nefārius* (“execrable, abominable”), from *nefās* (“something contrary to divine law, an impious deed, sin, crime”), from *ne-* (“not”) + *fās* (“the dictates of religion, divine law”), which is related to Latin *for* (“to speak, to say”) and…

core.definition: In Genesis, mighty beings or giants who lived on earth before and after the flood, possibly offspring of the sons of God and human women.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: NEF-ih-lim. The 'ph' is /f/, and the last two syllables are short and light, not 'LEEM'. Some Americans say 'NEF-ih-lym'.

nuance.connotation: Mysterious, ominous; associated with violence and ancient legend.
nuance.usage_note: Used in Bible study, theology, and in fantasy and conspiracy-themed media. Treated as a plural, with 'Nephilim' sometimes also used as a group name. A singular is sometimes 'Nephil' but rarely used.

distinctions.note: Giants means large people generally; Nephilim is the specific Hebrew term, whose exact meaning is debated.
Rephaim is another Hebrew term for ancient peoples or shades of the dead, often also translated giants.
The Anakim were a specific people of Canaan, said to be tall, while Nephilim are mentioned in primeval history.

examples.everyday: I read an article about who the Nephilim were in Genesis, and I was fascinated.
examples.professional: Today's seminar will compare Jewish and Christian interpretations of the Nephilim.
examples.analytical: The identity of the Nephilim remains disputed, with readings ranging from fallen angels' offspring to descendants of Seth or powerful human rulers.

nuance.analogy: They are like a legendary figure at the edge of the map: named, but their story is left unclear.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew nefilim, likely from naphal 'to fall', with meaning debated, perhaps 'fallen ones'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'neh-FEEL-im'.
Using it as a singular noun without noting it's plural.
Treating its meaning as settled.
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on earth in those days, when the sons of God had children with the daughters of men, who became mighty men of renown. Numbers 13:33 has the spies report seeing Nephilim in Canaan, descendants of Anak, compared to whom they felt like grasshoppers. The Hebrew nephilim may relate to naphal, 'to fall', though the meaning is debated.

nephilim.etymology: Borrowed from Hebrew *נְפִילִים* (“nefilim, fallen ones”), plural of *נָפִיל* (“nafíl, fallen one”).

senses.definition: Embedded.
Successively fitted one inside another.
(Of a lexical item) contained within a dictionary entry as a subordinate term of the main headword.

core.definition: Placed inside another item of the same kind, like a set of bowls stacked inside each other or a model inside a larger model.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NES. The -ed ending is pronounced as an extra syllable, so the word has two syllables after the stress, not one. Do not drop the ending and say NEST.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday speech nested is an ordinary adjective for things like nested mixing bowls or nested folders. Among data scientists and statisticians it has precise meanings: a nested model is a special case of a larger model, and nested data has levels such as students within classrooms. Americans use nested in technical talk, and embedded is a near alternative.

distinctions.note: Embedded emphasizes being placed within something larger to serve a function, while nested emphasizes a hierarchy of containers fitting inside each other.
Hierarchical describes the overall tree-like structure of a system, while nested describes one item sitting inside another.

examples.everyday: We have a set of nested mixing bowls in the cabinet, so they stack neatly.
examples.professional: The reduced model is nested within the full regression, so we can compare the two with a likelihood ratio test.
examples.analytical: In this nested design, each student belongs to exactly one classroom, so the observations are not independent and a multilevel model is required.

nuance.analogy: Like Russian dolls, each one fitting neatly inside the next.
nuance.etymology: From the verb nest, to fit one thing inside another, from Old English nest.
common_mistakes: Dropping the -ed ending so the word sounds like nest.
Using nested to mean just in a box, when it means fitting inside a container of the same type.

senses.definition: Variation or deviation generated by random fluctuations.
Various sounds, usually unwanted or unpleasant.
senses.example: He knew that it was trash day, when the garbage collectors made all the noise.

senses.definition: Any sound.
senses.example: The sudden noise made everyone jump.

senses.definition: Sound or signal generated by random fluctuations.
Any part of a signal or data that reduces the clarity, precision, or quality of the desired output.
senses.example: signal-to-noise ratio

senses.definition: Unwanted fuss or bustle; useless activity.
The measured level of variation in gene expression among cells, regardless of source, within a supposedly identical population.
Rumor or complaint.
senses.example: The problems with the new computer system are causing a lot of noise at Head Office.

senses.definition: Speech that is suggestive of an attitude or opinion.
A genre of rock music that uses static and other non-musical sounds, also influenced by art rock.
To make a noise; to sound.
To spread news of; to spread as rumor or gossip.
senses.example: an ugly story that was being noised about in newsrooms across the nation

core.definition: Unwanted or unpleasant sound; in statistics, random variation that obscures the true signal in data.

pronunciation.tip: The word has one syllable, with a diphthong that starts in the back of the mouth and glides toward ih. The provided IPA with the non-syllabic mark is unnecessary for learners; say it as one smooth sound ending in a voiced z.

nuance.connotation: negative in everyday speech, where noise means unwanted sound; neutral in statistics, where it is a technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say noise for any unwanted sound, such as traffic, neighbors, or construction. In data work, noise means random error or irrelevant variation. Phrases like too much noise or background noise are common, and the verb to noise about something (spread a rumor) is rare and literary.

distinctions.note: Sound is neutral and can be pleasant; noise usually implies something unwanted or confusing.
In data science, signal is the meaningful pattern and noise is the random variation around it.
Static often refers to electrical interference or a crackle in a radio or phone; noise is broader.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the noise from the construction next door woke me up this morning.
examples.professional: The dashboard looks noisy, so let's smooth the weekly data before we report the trend.
examples.analytical: A model that fits the noise rather than the underlying signal will generalize poorly to new observations.

nuance.analogy: Noise is like a crowded room in which you try to hear one friend; the friend is the signal, and the chatter is the noise.
nuance.etymology: From Old French noise, 'quarrel, outcry', probably from Latin nausea, 'seasickness, disgust'.
common_mistakes: Using noise as a countable noun without thinking, as in 'a noise' for every sound; this is fine, but 'noises' is more natural for many separate sounds.
Confusing noise with noisy by using the adjective form in the noun position.

noise.etymology: From Middle English *noyse*, *noise*, from Old French *noise* (“a dispute, wrangle, strife, noise”), of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: The state of being normative.
The state of being a norm.
That which is normative.

core.definition: The quality of setting or following standards of what is considered right, proper, or expected, as opposed to merely describing what is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third-from-last syllable, TIV, and the middle syllables are weak, so 'muh' and 'uh' should be reduced to schwa. Avoid giving every syllable equal weight, and keep the r clearly rhotic in 'nor'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a technical term in philosophy and ethics, with no emotional charge by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy, law, sociology, and ethics classes or papers, where it contrasts with descriptiveness. In everyday speech people say 'standards' or 'expectations' instead. It can sound pretentious outside academic settings.

distinctions.note: Normativity concerns what ought to be, while normalcy describes what is statistically typical or usual.
Normality is the state of being usual or ordinary, with no sense of moral obligation or standard.

examples.everyday: My sister says the whole idea of what a good parent should be is pure normativity, not something you can measure.
examples.professional: Before we build the fairness model, we need to agree on the normativity of the labels, meaning what counts as a correct outcome for users.
examples.analytical: Hume's distinction between is and ought exposes the normativity embedded in any account that treats natural facts as sufficient grounds for moral claims.

nuance.analogy: Descriptive statements are like a map showing where roads are; normativity is the rule that says which road you should take.
nuance.etymology: From 'normative,' from Latin norma, a carpenter's square or rule, plus the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Using 'normativity' to mean 'normality' or 'what is typical'; it refers to standards, not frequency.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'nor-MA-tiv-i-ty' instead of placing primary stress on TIV.

senses.definition: Being or relating to a form of Evangelical Protestant pastoral counseling based upon the Bible and focused on Christ.

core.definition: Relating to a Protestant form of pastoral counseling that instructs and admonishes people using Scripture, with Christ at the center.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, THET, and th is voiceless as in 'think.' Do not pronounce it as 'NOO-thetic'; the stress is in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive within evangelical circles; outsiders may find it technical or unfamiliar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nouthetic almost only in evangelical Protestant and biblical counseling contexts, such as seminary courses, church counseling programs, and books on pastoral care. It is tied to the approach of Jay Adams, who promoted directive, Scripture-based counseling. Outside those settings, people would simply say biblical counseling or pastoral counseling, and using nouthetic in casual talk would sound specialized.

distinctions.note: Biblical counseling is the broader, more common term; nouthetic refers specifically to the admonishing, instructing model developed from the Greek word noutheteō.
Nondirective counseling, associated with Carl Rogers, lets the client lead; nouthetic counseling is directive and tells people what Scripture requires.

examples.everyday: Our church just started a nouthetic counseling group, so people can talk through problems with Scripture.
examples.professional: The seminary's counseling course compares nouthetic methods with more therapeutic approaches.
examples.analytical: A nouthetic reading of pastoral care stresses the authority of Scripture to confront and correct the believer.

nuance.analogy: Nouthetic counseling is like a coach who points out your mistakes and shows you the playbook, rather than only asking how you feel about the game.
nuance.etymology: From the Greek noutheteō, 'to admonish, instruct, put in mind.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'NOO-thetic'; the stress is on THET.
Confusing nouthetic with nondirective or therapeutic; the word specifically means directive and Scripture-based.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb noutheteō means to admonish, warn, or instruct, and it gives the modern term its root. Romans 15:14 describes believers as able to instruct one another. Colossians 1:28 speaks of Paul admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that each person may be presented mature in Christ.

core.definition: A minor prophet of Israel and the author of the shortest book in the Old Testament, which warns Edom of judgment for its cruelty toward Judah.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, DYE. The final 'iah' is a reduced 'uh' sound, so do not say a long 'ee' at the end.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Obadiah is a biblical name used both for the prophet and for other people in Scripture. Americans know it mostly from church settings and Bible study, and it is a traditional name still used in some families.

examples.everyday: Our pastor's sermon on Sunday was from Obadiah, which I did not expect since it is such a short book.
examples.professional: In the seminar, we compared Obadiah's oracle against Edom with the oracles of Amos and Jeremiah.
examples.analytical: The book of Obadiah consists of a single chapter of twenty-one verses that combines a judgment oracle against Edom with a vision of the restoration of Israel.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Obadyah', meaning 'servant of Yahweh'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which makes it sound like 'oh-buh-DYE-uh' with the wrong rhythm; the stress is on DYE.
Confusing the prophet with other Obadiahs in the Bible, such as the steward of King Ahab in 1 Kings 18.
nuance.biblical_note: Obadiah, the prophet, is one of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. The book of Obadiah pronounces judgment on Edom for standing aloof when Jerusalem was attacked and for rejoicing over Judah's ruin. Verse 15 announces that the day of the LORD is near for all nations. The name means 'servant of the LORD' in Hebrew, and Obadiah the steward of Ahab, in 1 Kings 18:3-4, is a different man who protected the prophets of the LORD.

senses.definition: The alteration of computer code to preserve its behavior while concealing its structure and intent.
senses.example: You need to turn on obfuscation for these classes.

senses.definition: The act or process of obfuscating, or obscuring the perception of something; the concept of concealing the meaning of a communication by making it more confusing and harder to interpret.
senses.example: You need to turn on obfuscation for these classes.

senses.definition: Confusion, bewilderment, or a baffled state resulting from something obfuscated, or made more opaque and muddled with the intent to obscure information.
A single instance of intentionally obscuring the meaning of something to make it more difficult to grasp.
senses.example: During the debate, the candidate sighed at his opponent's obfuscations.

core.definition: The deliberate act of making something confusing or hard to understand, in order to hide the truth or meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on SKAY, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle 'fuh' is reduced, and the final -tion sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests deception or evasion, though in computing it is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people rarely say 'obfuscation'; they say 'runaround' or 'double talk.' It appears in journalism, law, politics, and software engineering. In code discussions, the word is neutral and describes a technique rather than a dishonest act.

distinctions.note: Ambiguity is a property of language that can be read more than one way; obfuscation is a deliberate act of making meaning harder to access.
Evasion is avoiding a direct answer; obfuscation is more about burying the truth in confusing detail.

examples.everyday: Whenever my landlord starts talking about fees, it's just obfuscation, so I always ask for the amount in writing.
examples.professional: Our security team uses code obfuscation to protect the proprietary logic in the mobile app, but it doesn't replace real access controls.
examples.analytical: Lyotard's critique of technical language suggests that obfuscation can serve power by making specialized discourse appear neutral while excluding ordinary citizens.

nuance.analogy: Obfuscation is like a magician's misdirection: the trick is hidden not by being secret, but by flooding your attention with distracting details.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin obfuscatio, from obfuscare, 'to darken'.
common_mistakes: Confusing obfuscation with confusion; obfuscation implies a deliberate act, while confusion may be accidental.
Mispronouncing it with stress on the first syllable, as in 'AHB-fuh-scay-shun'; the main stress is on SKAY.

obfuscation.etymology: From Middle English *obfuscacioun*, from Latin *obfuscatio*, from *obfuscāre* (“to darken”), from *ob* (“over”) + *fuscāre* (“to make dark”), from *fuscus* (“dark”).

senses.definition: Able to be observed.
senses.example: The strange new star was at the edge of the observable universe.

senses.definition: Deserving to be observed; worth regarding; remarkable.
Any physical property that can be observed and measured directly and not derived from other properties.
senses.example: Temperature is an observable but entropy is derived.

core.definition: Able to be seen, noticed or measured; capable of being observed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZUR, and the final -able reduces to a light 'uh-buhl', with the L as a syllabic sound. Avoid stressing the first syllable as in OB-serv-able.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use observable in everyday speech ('an observable change') and in science and engineering ('observable behavior'). The sense 'worth noticing' is common in writing but Americans more often say 'notable' or 'noticeable' in conversation. In technical contexts the noun form refers to a measurable property of a system.

distinctions.note: Visible refers to what the eye can see, while observable can also include things measured by instruments or inferred from evidence.
Noticeable means easy for people to perceive, while observable is broader and may require careful measurement or study.

examples.everyday: The swelling has gone down, but there's no observable difference in the bruise yet.
examples.professional: The error rate is now observable on the dashboard, so we can finally see the regression as it happens.
examples.analytical: A hypothesis is meaningful only if it makes observable predictions that could, in principle, count against it.

nuance.analogy: A footprint is observable; the animal that made it is not directly observable but can be inferred from the evidence.
nuance.etymology: From Latin observabilis, from observare, 'to watch over'.
common_mistakes: Using observable to describe a person who is watchful; the right word is observant.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second, as in OB-ser-vable.

senses.definition: Related to the occult; pertaining to mysticism, magic, or astrology.
Esoteric.
Secret; hidden from general knowledge; undetected.
senses.example: occult blood loss; occult cancer

senses.definition: Not visible, but chemically detectable.
senses.example: occult blood in the urine

senses.definition: Supernatural affairs.
To cover or hide from view.
senses.example: The Earth occults the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

senses.definition: To dissimulate, conceal, or obfuscate.

core.definition: Relating to magic, astrology, or supernatural practices; also, hidden or secret from ordinary knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KULT. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final t is clearly pronounced, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: often negative or suspicious, suggesting secret or dangerous practices; neutral when used in academic or historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use occult in phrases about magic, witchcraft, or supernatural practices, and in fiction and film. Saying occult studies or occult history in a classroom is neutral, but calling someone occult can sound accusatory. The noun form is rare in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Mystical describes a sense of spiritual union or insight and can be positive; occult usually refers to magic or secret practices and can be negative.
Hidden is a general word for not visible; occult carries the extra sense of secret knowledge or supernatural matters.

examples.everyday: My roommate loves horror movies, and she always watches the ones with occult themes.
examples.professional: Our marketing team decided against using occult imagery in the new campaign because it might offend customers.
examples.analytical: Historians of early modern Europe often distinguish between occult philosophy and natural science, though the two overlapped.

nuance.analogy: Like a backstage door, it leads to knowledge most people cannot see from the audience.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occultus, 'hidden,' past participle of occulere, 'to cover over.'
common_mistakes: Using occult as a synonym for culture or cult in ordinary speech.
Mispronouncing it with a silent final t or stressing the first syllable.

senses.definition: In an extemporaneous manner; without careful thought, preparation, or investigation.
senses.example: I cannot think of any good examples off the top of my head, but give me a couple of hours and I'm sure I could come up with something.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see off,‎ top,‎ head.

core.definition: Without careful thought, preparation, or research; from immediate memory or first impressions.

pronunciation.respelling: awf thuh tahp uhv my HED
pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'head', and 'off', 'top', and 'my' carry lighter stress. In fast speech, 'of my' is reduced to 'uhv my', and 'the top' links to sound like 'thuh-tahp'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. It shows honesty about not having checked the facts, and it sounds casual and friendly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in conversation when giving a quick answer or estimate, such as when someone asks for a recommendation. It signals that you are not certain, so it is polite and modest. A natural reply is 'That's helpful, I'll double-check later.' It is common in meetings and casual talk, but in formal reports you would say 'a preliminary estimate' instead.

distinctions.note: Offhand means done casually and without thought, and can sound dismissive; off the top of my head is a more polite way to say you are giving an immediate answer.
Off the cuff means spoken without preparation, often in a speech; off the top of my head focuses on memory and immediate recall.

collocations: off the top of my head
answer off the top of my head
guess off the top of my head
say off the top of my head
estimate off the top of my head

examples.everyday: Do you know a good Italian place nearby? Off the top of my head, I'd say Luigi's on Fifth Street.
examples.professional: Off the top of my head, I think the deployment takes about two days, but I'll confirm the timeline with the ops team.
examples.analytical: Off the top of my head, the argument seems plausible, but a careful reading of the primary sources would be needed to test it.

nuance.analogy: Speaking off the top of my head is like pulling a card from the top of a deck without looking at the rest.
nuance.etymology: Idiomatic, from the everyday image of thoughts appearing at the top of the mind.
common_mistakes: Saying 'from the top of my head', which is a common error; the standard phrase is 'off the top of my head'.
Using it in formal reports where careful, verified answers are expected.
Stressing 'top' more than 'head'; the main stress is on 'head'.

conversation.text: Off the top of my head, I'd say about two hundred customers.
I don't know her number off the top of my head.
Off the top of my head, I can think of three good restaurants nearby.

senses.definition: A value in a statistical sample which does not fit a pattern that describes most other data points; specifically, a value that lies 1.5 IQR beyond the upper or lower quartile.
A person or thing situated away from the main body or outside its proper place.
An exception.
A part of a formation separated from the rest of the formation by erosion.

core.definition: A data point that lies far outside the general pattern of a dataset, or a person or thing that is unusual.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OUT, the first syllable. The final -ier is pronounced like the American 'er' with a rhotic r, so it sounds like 'lye-er' and not 'lye-ay.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In everyday use it can be a mild compliment or a neutral label for an exception.
nuance.usage_note: In data science, Americans use outlier in a precise statistical sense and often describe how it was detected or handled. In everyday speech, people use it less often but may say 'an outlier' for an unusual case or person. Saying 'That's an outlier' in a meeting usually means the value should be checked before it is included.

distinctions.note: An anomaly is any unexpected or unusual observation, often in monitoring; an outlier is a value far from the bulk of a dataset, though the terms are often used interchangeably.
An exception breaks a rule or pattern, while an outlier is a numerical or statistical point far from the rest of the data.

examples.everyday: Our neighborhood's average income looks high, but that's just one outlier, a few very rich families.
examples.professional: Before we fit the model, let's flag the outliers in the sales data and check whether they're real or entry errors.
examples.analytical: A sample mean is sensitive to a single outlier, which is why the median is often preferred for skewed distributions.

nuance.analogy: An outlier is like one tall player on a youth soccer team: the rest of the team looks similar, but that one player stands far above the others.
nuance.etymology: From out plus the verb lie, referring to something lying outside the main group.
common_mistakes: Removing outliers automatically; a real extreme value may be important information.
Mispronouncing the final syllable; it is 'er,' not 'ay.'

senses.definition: An additional sample of a subpopulation, above and beyond the portion of a main sample that already belongs to that subpopulation.
To sample additional members of a subpopulation, above and beyond the members included in the main sample.
To sample a signal at a frequency well above its Nyquist rate.

core.definition: An extra sample drawn from a subgroup so it has enough cases for reliable analysis, beyond what a main sample would include.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable in the noun, and the final -ple is a weak syllable. The verb shifts stress to the second syllable: oh-ver-SAM-pul, so stress differs by part of speech.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Oversampling is standard vocabulary in survey research, polling, clinical trials and machine learning. Americans use it as a technical term, usually in the context of analysis plans or methods sections. Outside of statistics, it sounds jargony.

distinctions.note: Subsampling draws a smaller portion from an existing sample, whereas oversampling draws extra cases from a subgroup to increase its representation.
In signal processing, upsampling means increasing the sampling rate by inserting samples; oversampling can refer to sampling above the Nyquist rate, which is a related but distinct idea.

examples.everyday: My cousin works at a polling firm, and they oversample young voters so the results for that age group actually mean something.
examples.professional: We oversampled customers from the new region to get enough data for a reliable churn model.
examples.analytical: Oversampling a subgroup inflates its weight in the raw estimate unless the analysis is reweighted to recover population parameters.

nuance.analogy: Like taking extra photos of a rare bird so you can study its features, rather than relying on the few you happened to snap.
nuance.etymology: From over- plus sample; the statistical sense developed in the twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in the verb form, saying oh-ver-SAM-pul for the noun instead of OH-ver-sam-pul.
Confusing oversampling with simply having a large sample; the point is to increase a specific subgroup.

senses.definition: Excessively zealous; excessively enthusiastic or fervent.
senses.example: With his overzealous attempts to impress, he only managed to annoy her.

core.definition: Too enthusiastic or eager about something, often to the point of causing problems or annoyance for others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'ZEL', and the first syllable is a reduced 'ver'. The final 'ous' is a reduced 'us', not 'ous' as in 'house'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly negative; it suggests enthusiasm that has gone too far.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overzealous to criticize someone who is too eager, such as an overzealous referee or an overzealous salesperson. It is often said with a bit of humor or mild annoyance. Saying 'a little overzealous' is a polite way to describe someone without being harsh.

distinctions.note: Enthusiastic is usually positive, while overzealous means enthusiasm has gone beyond what is wise or welcome.
Zealous can be positive, but overzealous always carries criticism of excess.

examples.everyday: The waiter was a little overzealous, refilling my water every five minutes.
examples.professional: The compliance team was overzealous in flagging minor issues, which slowed the whole release.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that overzealous regulation can stifle innovation without improving public safety.

nuance.analogy: An overzealous person is like a dog that wags so hard it knocks over the coffee table.
nuance.etymology: From 'over' and 'zealous', from Greek 'zēlos' (zeal, fervor).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'zee' sound rather than reduced 'ver' plus stressed 'ZEL'.
Using overzealous as a positive word for enthusiasm, when it usually signals too much.

senses.definition: A manuscript or document that has been erased or scraped clean, for reuse of the paper, parchment, vellum, or other medium on which it was written.
Memory that has been erased and re-written.
The partial erasure of or superimposition on an older society or culture by a newer one.
Something bearing the traces of an earlier, erased form.
A text with several layers of meaning, especially pertaining to different points in time.
Circular features believed to be lunar craters that have been obliterated by later volcanic activity.
Geological features thought to be related to features or effects below the surface.
To scrape clean, as in parchment, for reuse.
On paper: to reuse, often by erasure or change of pen direction or color. Especially fueled by Earth Day.
senses.example: Typically refers to a multi-layered work, e.g.: new ads covering old on a roadside sign.

core.definition: A manuscript or surface that was written on, scraped clean, and written on again, with traces of the older writing still visible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'p' in 'imp' is clearly pronounced, and the final syllable rhymes with 'best'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests history, layering, and the survival of older meanings beneath newer ones.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use palimpsest mainly in academic, literary, and historical writing, for manuscripts studied in libraries or for layers of culture and memory. In casual speech it would sound overly bookish. Figuratively, you might describe a city's streets as a palimpsest of different eras. A natural reply in conversation is simply to ask what the layers reveal.

distinctions.note: A manuscript is any handwritten document, while a palimpsest is specifically one whose original text was erased and overwritten.
Layer is a general word for something stacked; palimpsest emphasizes writing or history that remains partly visible beneath later additions.

examples.everyday: That old building is a palimpsest, with its different paint colors showing through the newer walls.
examples.professional: The archive team used multispectral imaging to read the palimpsest and recover the erased text beneath.
examples.analytical: The city's identity is a palimpsest in which colonial, industrial, and modern strata remain partly legible.

nuance.analogy: A palimpsest is like a whiteboard that was erased but never fully cleaned: the old notes still show faintly under the new ones.
nuance.etymology: From Greek palimpsestos, 'scraped again', from palin, 'again', and psestos, 'scraped'.
common_mistakes: Using palimpsest for any document, instead of one that was scraped and reused.
Mispronouncing the middle as 'PAL-im-sest' with the 'p' dropped.

palimpsest.etymology: From Latin *palimpsēstus*, from Ancient Greek *παλίμψηστος* (“scraped again”).

senses.definition: Originally, one's oath or word of honor, given as a condition of release from custody; now specifically, describing the release of a former prisoner under certain conditions, especially the promise of good behavior.
senses.example: He will be on parole for nearly two more years.

senses.definition: Conditional release of a prisoner (now especially before the end of a custodial sentence), or the term or state of such release; the system governing such releases.
Language in use, as opposed to language as a system.
The permission for a foreigner who does not meet the technical requirements for a visa to be allowed to enter the U.S. on humanitarian grounds.
A word of honor, especially given by a prisoner of war, to not engage in combat if released.
A watchword or code phrase; a password given only to officers, distinguished from the countersign, which is given to all guards.
To be released on parole.
To conditionally release an incarcerated person before completion of their sentence, subject to ongoing legal custody or supervision and compliance with specified terms of release.

core.definition: Conditional early release of a prisoner under supervision, based on promised good behavior; to release someone on such terms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable ROHL, with a rhotic r and a clear l at the end. Do not add a vowel before the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal and official contexts; it can carry a negative association with crime and supervision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parole in courts, news reports, and criminal justice discussions. It refers to a supervised early release, not to a full pardon. People say he is up for parole or he was paroled. Probation is the related term for someone who is supervised instead of imprisoned.

distinctions.note: Probation is a sentence served in the community instead of prison; parole is release from prison before the sentence ends.
A pardon forgives the crime and removes the legal consequences; parole is a conditional release that continues supervision.

examples.everyday: My cousin was released on parole last year and has to check in with his officer every week.
examples.professional: The case manager reminded the client that his parole conditions include regular drug testing.
examples.analytical: The debate over parole reform often turns on whether rehabilitation or public safety should guide the decision.

nuance.analogy: Parole is like a leash on a dog let out of the yard: free to move, but still watched and required to come back if the rules are broken.
nuance.etymology: From Old French parole, word, from Latin parabola, speech, from Greek parabole; the legal sense began with a prisoner's word of honor.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like the English word pa-ROLE with a long o and a hard second syllable in a different place; the stress is on the single syllable.
Confusing parole with probation, which is a different sentence.

parole.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *parole* (“word, formal promise”), from Old French *parole*, from Late Latin *parabola* (“speech”), from Ancient Greek *παραβολή*.

senses.definition: The condition of being penitent; a feeling of regret or remorse for doing wrong or sinning.

core.definition: Deep sorrow and regret for having done wrong or sinned, often with a desire to make things right.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowels. The -ence ending is a weak 'uns', not 'ance' or 'ents'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or solemn. It describes sincere sorrow for wrongdoing and is often used in religious or moral contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use penitence in religious writing, moral discussion, and literature. In daily speech they would say regret, remorse, or sorrow. Penitence can sound solemn, so it fits a sermon, an essay, or a formal apology better than casual talk.

distinctions.note: Remorse is a general feeling of guilt and is common in everyday speech. Penitence is more formal and implies a moral or religious turning toward making amends.
Penitence is the inner feeling of sorrow, while penance is the outward act done to express it.

examples.everyday: He apologized with real penitence after he broke the vase, and he offered to pay for a new one.
examples.professional: Our postmortem did not blame anyone, but the team showed penitence for skipping the review step.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats penitence not merely as an emotion but as a turning of the will toward God, which is why sorrow alone is insufficient.

nuance.analogy: Penitence is like a heavy heart that turns around and walks back toward home: the sorrow is the feeling, and the return is the change.
nuance.etymology: From Latin paenitentia, 'repentance', from paenitere 'to repent'.
common_mistakes: Using penitence for the act of penance rather than the feeling of sorrow.
Confusing penitence with penitentiary, the word for a prison.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV Bible uses repentance rather than penitence for the Greek metanoia, meaning a change of mind and heart toward God. Key passages are Matthew 3:8, where John the Baptist calls for fruit that befits repentance; Luke 15:7, where heaven rejoices over a sinner who repents; and 2 Corinthians 7:10, where Paul says godly grief produces a repentance without regret.

traditions.view: Orthodox teach that penitence is a continual change of heart and mind, expressed in confession, prayer, fasting, and the life of the Church. Sorrow for sin is seen as part of the healing of the whole person.

Catholics teach that penitence includes contrition, the sorrow and resolve not to sin again, which is joined to confession and satisfaction in the sacrament of Penance. Contrition is considered essential to forgiveness.

Most Protestants teach that penitence is a sincere repentance that flows from faith and the grace of God, rather than a work that earns forgiveness. Lutherans and Reformed differ on how the law and the gospel relate to sorrow for sin.

penitence.etymology: First attested circa 13th century, from Middle English *penitence*, from Old French *penitence*, from Latin *paenitentia* (“repentance, penitence”), from *paenitēns* (“penitent”), present active participle of *paeniteō* (“regret, repent”).

senses.definition: Lasting or remaining active throughout the year, for multiple years, or all the time.
senses.example: a perennial stream

senses.definition: Continuing without cessation or intermission for several years, or for an undetermined or infinite period; never-ending or never failing; perpetual, unceasing.
senses.example: His artwork has a perennial beauty.

senses.definition: Appearing or recurring again and again; recurrent.
senses.example: a perennial candidate in elections

senses.definition: Of a plant: active throughout the year, or having a life cycle of more than two growing seasons.
Appearing again each year; annual.
A thing that lasts forever.
A person or thing (such as a problem) that appears or returns regularly.
A plant that is active throughout the year, or has a life cycle of more than two growing seasons.

core.definition: Lasting or recurring year after year, or happening again and again over a long time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REN, the second syllable. The final syllable is reduced to 'ul', so it sounds like 'REN-ee-ul', not 'per-EN-ee-al'. The provided IPA with the dot and '(ə)l' is British-style or unclear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive for a lasting plant or tradition and negative for a recurring problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'perennial' for flowers that return each year, and for recurring issues like 'a perennial problem' or 'a perennial favorite'. It is common in news, business and everyday talk. Saying 'perennial' about a person who keeps appearing, like 'perennial candidate', is a casual but widely understood usage.

distinctions.note: An annual plant lives only one growing season, while a perennial comes back year after year.
Recurrent is a neutral term for happening again, while perennial often implies a long-lasting, persistent quality.

examples.everyday: Tomatoes are annuals, but the peonies in my yard are perennial and come back every spring.
examples.professional: Budget overruns are a perennial problem on this team, so we need a better forecasting process.
examples.analytical: The question of free will is perennial, returning in every century under new vocabulary.

nuance.analogy: A perennial is like a loyal friend who shows up at every family gathering year after year.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perennis, 'lasting through the year', from per 'through' and annus 'year'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'annual' when talking about plants.
Stressing the first syllable as 'PER-en-ial'.

perennial.etymology: The adjective is borrowed from Latin *perennis* (“lasting through the whole year or for several years, perennial; continual, everlasting, perpetual”) + *-al*.

senses.definition: Liable to perish, especially naturally subject to quick decomposition or decay.
senses.example: perishable goods

senses.definition: That which perishes or is short-lived.
Food that does not keep for long.

core.definition: Likely to decay, spoil, or go bad quickly, especially food; also short-lived or not built to last.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PAIR. The -shuh-buhl ending is weak and quick, and the r should be clear, not swallowed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It describes a quality, often with a note of concern for spoiling or loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perishable mainly in shopping, grocery, shipping, and business settings, such as perishable goods or perishable items. In a store, a clerk might say these are perishable, so keep them cold. The noun form is rare and mostly literary.

distinctions.note: Spoiled describes food that has already gone bad; perishable describes food that is likely to go bad soon.
Durable means strong and long-lasting, the opposite quality of perishable.
Fresh describes food in a good, recently harvested state; perishable describes the risk of spoilage.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the milk and the strawberries? They're both perishable, so put them in the cooler bag.
examples.professional: Our shipping contract has a strict cold-chain requirement for perishable products to avoid spoilage claims.
examples.analytical: The author compares human memory to perishable goods, which decay unless they are carefully preserved.

nuance.analogy: A perishable item is like a carton of milk in a warm kitchen: it is fine now, but it has a short window before it turns.
nuance.etymology: From perish plus the suffix -able, meaning able to be perished or liable to decay.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as pe-RISH-uh-bul.
Using perishable to describe people or ideas in everyday speech, where it sounds strange or overly technical.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind perishable is phthartos (subject to decay, corruptible), describing things and bodies that wear out and decay. Matthew 6:19 warns against storing up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, so that treasure is safe in heaven. 1 Corinthians 15:53 says this perishable nature must put on the imperishable, linking the future resurrection to the transformation of the mortal body. 1 Peter 1:18 says believers were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.

senses.definition: In AI: A measure of how well a language model predicts text; lower perplexity means better prediction.
The state or quality of being perplexed.
Something that perplexes.
A measure of the accuracy with which a probability distribution or model predicts a sample.

core.definition: In AI, a score measuring how well a language model predicts text; lower perplexity means the model predicts the next word more accurately.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLEK, and the final syllable is a light tee. Americans reduce the middle vowel, so avoid saying the middle syllable clearly as sih-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In AI it is a technical measure; in everyday speech it means confusion.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI teams, Americans say perplexity almost always in the technical sense of model evaluation. In everyday talk the word is formal, so people usually say confusion. Note that a lower perplexity score is better, which often surprises learners.

distinctions.note: Confusion is everyday and general; perplexity in the AI sense is a precise numerical metric and is not a state of mind.
Accuracy measures how often predictions are correct; perplexity measures how uncertain the model is about the next token, so lower is better.

examples.everyday: I felt a sense of perplexity when the instructions changed twice in one afternoon.
examples.professional: Our new model reduced validation perplexity from 42 to 31, so it predicts the held-out text much better.
examples.analytical: Perplexity is a useful metric, but it does not directly measure whether a model's outputs are factually correct or useful.

nuance.analogy: Perplexity is like a quiz score for a model: the less surprised it is by the correct next word, the lower the score.
nuance.etymology: From perplex, from Latin perplexus, entangled, with the -ity noun suffix.
common_mistakes: Assuming higher perplexity is better; in language models, lower perplexity means better prediction.
Using perplexity to mean complexity in everyday talk, where it sounds formal and sometimes odd.

perplexity.etymology: From Middle English *perplexite*, borrowed from Middle French *perplexité* or post-classical Latin *perplexitās*, from *perplexus* (“entangled”).

conversation.text: Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; lower is better.
Perplexity numbers aren't directly comparable across models with different tokenizers.
She stared at the error message in perplexity; the code hadn't changed at all.

senses.definition: Of a person: having a pleasing appearance; attractive; handsome.
Of a person: having a pleasant manner; amiable, friendly.
Synonym of personal (“done in person, without an intermediary”).
Being a legal person and thus able to maintain a plea in court, or to hold some property or right.

core.definition: Pleasant, friendly, and easy to talk to; having an agreeable, approachable manner.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. In fast speech the middle syllable is often nearly silent, so it sounds like 'PURS-nuh-buhl', and the final -able is a weak schwa, not 'ay-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone for being warm and easy to deal with, but it is more modest than 'charming' or 'brilliant'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for people who are easy to get along with, especially in job interviews, reference letters, and casual talk about coworkers or neighbors. It describes a person, not a thing. The older sense of 'good-looking' is rarely used today in everyday American English.

distinctions.note: Friendly describes warmth in general, while personable adds the idea of being pleasant to deal with in a professional or first-meeting setting.
Charming suggests a strong, delightful appeal that can seem polished, while personable is plainer and more practical.

examples.everyday: Our new neighbor is really personable, so we invited her over for dinner next week.
examples.professional: The hiring manager said Dana was personable and clear in the interview, which helped her stand out from the other candidates.
examples.analytical: A personable person, in Aristotle's terms, shows settled goodwill in ordinary conduct rather than a performance staged for others.

nuance.analogy: A personable person is like a porch light left on: easy to approach and welcoming.
nuance.etymology: From person, from Latin persona (mask, character), plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'per-SOH-nuh-bul'.
Confusing it with 'personal', which means private or individual.

personable.etymology: From Late Middle English *personable*, *personabil* (“having a pleasing appearance, handsome”), and then from both of the following:

senses.definition: Clearly expressed, easy to understand; lucid.
(Of a language or notation) the process of inference from premises to conclusion is explicitly laid out.
That can be seen through clearly; that lets light through.

core.definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand; lucid. Used mostly for writing, arguments, and explanations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPIK. Don't stress the first syllable or pronounce it as 'pair'; the first vowel is reduced to a short 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises writing or speech that is clear and precise, and it is rarely used for people in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic, philosophical, legal, or technical writing, and in reviews of prose. In everyday speech they would say clear, easy to follow, or straightforward. Using it in casual conversation can sound showy.

distinctions.note: Clear is everyday and covers all kinds of clarity; perspicuous is more formal and specifically describes clarity of expression.
Lucid can describe a clear mind or a calm, sensible moment as well as writing, while perspicuous applies only to expression and explanation.
Perspicacious means having sharp insight into people or situations; perspicuous means clearly written or stated. The two are often confused.

examples.everyday: Her email was so perspicuous that I didn't have to ask a single follow-up question.
examples.professional: The design doc is perspicuous enough that a new engineer could implement the service without a meeting.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein sought a perspicuous notation in which the logical form of propositions would become visible.

nuance.analogy: A perspicuous text is like a clean window: you look straight through it and see the idea without noticing the glass.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perspicuus, 'transparent, clear,' from perspicere, 'to see through.'
common_mistakes: Confusing perspicuous (clear) with perspicacious (insightful about people).
Stressing the first syllable as in 'PER-spi-cuous'.

perspicuous.etymology: From Latin *perspicuus*, in turn from *perspiciō* (“see through”).

senses.definition: A restaurant that bakes and sells pizzas.

core.definition: A restaurant that makes and sells pizza, often a casual place where you can eat in or take food out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'REE'. Say the 'tz' sound as a single 'ts' blend, similar to 'pizza', and the final syllable is 'uh', not 'ee-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and casual. It suggests an inexpensive, friendly, family-style restaurant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pizzeria for a place that specializes in pizza, often a small local shop, and it is a normal everyday word. Larger chain restaurants are usually called pizza places or by the brand name. In casual talk people often just say 'pizza' or 'let's get pizza'.

distinctions.note: Pizza place is the more casual, everyday American phrase; pizzeria sounds slightly more traditional or Italian.
Restaurant is general; pizzeria names a specific type of restaurant.
Trattoria is an Italian family-style restaurant serving a wider menu; a pizzeria focuses on pizza.

examples.everyday: Let's grab dinner at that little pizzeria on Fifth Street; their garlic knots are great.
examples.professional: Our team lunch is at the pizzeria across from the office, so let's meet there at noon.
examples.analytical: The rise of the independent pizzeria in American cities reflects a shift toward local, craft-based dining.

nuance.analogy: A pizzeria is to pizza what a bakery is to bread: a shop built around one main product.
nuance.etymology: From Italian pizzeria, a pizza shop, from pizza.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the 'z' as a plain 'z' sound; in pizza and pizzeria it is a 'ts' sound.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PIT-suh-ree-uh'.

conversation.text: The pizzeria down the street sells pizza by the slice.
We ordered two large pies from our favorite pizzeria.
That little pizzeria makes its own dough every morning.

senses.definition: One who furnishes, fits, and repairs pipes and other apparatus for the conveyance of water, gas, or drainage.
senses.example: Mario and Luigi's profession is plumbers.

senses.definition: A person who investigates or prevents leaks of information.
Ellipsis of plumbers and firemen.
A urologist.
One who works in or with lead.
To botch or ruin.
To work as a plumber.
To work on (something) as a plumber.
To do, work, devise (something).
To equip (something) with plumbing.

core.definition: A worker who installs and repairs pipes, faucets, and drains in houses and buildings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the last syllable a weak, rhotic 'er' sound. Do not pronounce the 'b' from the root 'plumb.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it refers to a respected skilled trade, though calling someone a plumber in a joke can imply a rough, practical job.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'plumber' for any professional who fixes water pipes or drains, and calling one for an emergency at home is very normal. People also say 'plumber's helper' or 'plumbing company.' The phrase 'a plumber's crack' is a crude joke, so avoid repeating it in polite company.

distinctions.note: Plumber is the person; plumbing is the system of pipes or the trade.
An electrician works on wires and power; a plumber works on water, gas, and drainage.

examples.everyday: Our kitchen sink is leaking, so we need to call a plumber before the floor gets wet.
examples.professional: The property manager asked the plumber to inspect the building's water lines before the inspection.
examples.analytical: The plumber's trade depends on detailed knowledge of pressure, materials, and building codes, not only on manual skill.

nuance.analogy: A plumber is like a doctor for a house's circulatory system, diagnosing where the flow is blocked.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plumbarius, a worker in lead, from plumbum (lead), since early pipes were made of lead.
common_mistakes: Saying 'plum-ber' with a 'b' sound at the end.
Using 'plumber' for an electrical problem; Americans call that an electrician.

plumber.etymology: From Middle English *plumber*, from Old French *plummier* (French *plombier*); from Latin *plumbārius*, from *plumbum* (“lead or lead shot”).

conversation.text: We need to call a plumber; the water heater is leaking.
The plumber said he could come Tuesday morning.
Plumbers charge a lot for weekend visits.

senses.definition: Too deep to be plumbed.

core.definition: Too deep to be measured or reached, especially in a literary or figurative sense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the ending a short, unstressed 'lis.' The middle 'l' is clear, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests vast, mysterious depths.
nuance.usage_note: 'Plumbless' is rare in American speech and writing. It appears mostly in poetry, fiction, or deliberately elevated prose. Everyday speakers would say 'bottomless' or 'unfathomable' instead. Use it only when you want a literary effect.

distinctions.note: Bottomless is common and can be literal or figurative; plumbless is more literary and emphasizes that depth cannot be measured.
Unfathomable is widely used for things that cannot be understood; plumbless is closer to the literal idea of unmeasured depth.

examples.everyday: The ocean looked almost plumbless from the cliff, so we just stared at it for a while.
examples.professional: The report describes the plumbless uncertainty in the market, which makes forecasting difficult.
examples.analytical: The poem speaks of a plumbless grief that resists any attempt at measurement or consolation.

nuance.analogy: A plumbless sea is like a well with no visible bottom, where your weighted line never reaches the floor.
nuance.etymology: From plumb (a weight used to measure depth) plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using 'plumbless' in casual conversation, where 'bottomless' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing the 'b' in 'plumb' because of the spelling.

senses.definition: Exaggerated speech or gestures used for emphasis during a performance.

core.definition: Reward units earned through purchases that can be redeemed for discounts, products or other benefits, such as in a store's loyalty program.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a diphthong: 'oy' is a single glide from 'aw' to 'ee', not two separate sounds. Keep the final 'nts' cluster clear, without adding a vowel before the 's'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: points signal savings and value. The word is neutral in most contexts, but in a non-shopping sense it can mean sharp remarks or matters, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say points for loyalty or rewards credits at stores, airlines and credit cards, for example 'Do you have any points on your card?' At the register, a cashier may ask 'Do you want to use your points?' A natural reply is 'Yes, please' or 'Not today, thanks.'

distinctions.note: Coupons give a fixed discount on a specific item, while points accumulate over time and are redeemed for rewards.
Miles are the points used by airline and travel programs; points is the general term for most reward programs.

examples.everyday: I'm buying this at the grocery store because I still have enough points to get a discount.
examples.professional: Our finance team reported that the points redemption rate rose after we changed the reward tiers.
examples.analytical: Loyalty points function as a deferred form of price reduction, so their value depends on how easily consumers can redeem them.

nuance.analogy: Points are like tokens in an arcade: you collect them slowly, and you spend them later on something you want.
nuance.etymology: Plural of point, from Latin punctum, 'a prick or dot'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I have many points' in a shopping context without specifying the program; say 'I have a lot of points' or 'I have enough points' instead.
Confusing points with coupons; points are earned over time, not a one-time discount.

conversation.text: You earn two points for every dollar you spend.
I used my points to get twenty dollars off.
Do my points expire at the end of the year?

senses.definition: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.
senses.example: The precocious plant was already blooming flowers by day 4.

senses.definition: Exhibiting advanced skills and aptitudes at an abnormally early age.
senses.example: The precocious child began reading the newspaper at age four.

core.definition: Developing or showing skills, maturity or knowledge unusually early, especially in a child.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, -KOH-. The final syllables are reduced to 'shus', so do not pronounce a full 'ee' ending.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive when describing a talented child, but it can sound slightly negative if it implies a child is acting too grown-up or showing off.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'precocious' for children who read early, play an instrument well or speak like adults. Parents and teachers say it warmly, but calling a child 'precocious' to mean 'bratty' can also happen. It is less common for adults; for them, 'early-developing' or 'advanced for his age' is more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Gifted' describes high ability in general, while 'precocious' focuses specifically on developing that ability unusually early.
'Talented' describes skill without any reference to age; 'precocious' always implies that the skill appeared earlier than expected.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's six-year-old is so precocious that she already reads chapter books.
examples.professional: The school placed the precocious student in the advanced math track after her diagnostic test results.
examples.analytical: Mill treats precocious intellectual development as a test case for whether education shapes talent or merely reveals it.

nuance.analogy: A plant that blooms in early March while everything else is still frozen: it is ready before its season.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecox, 'ripening early', from prae 'before' and coquere 'to cook or ripen'.
