common_mistakes: Confusing 'precocious' with 'precious', which means valuable or dearly loved.
Stressing the final syllable as in 'pre-co-SHUS'; the stress is in the middle.

precocious.etymology: From Latin *praecox* (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from *praecoquō* (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from *prae* (“before”) + *coquō* (“to cook, boil, ripen”).

senses.definition: Someone who returns home from traveling or exile or who is welcomed back after disgrace, especially having repented of former extravagant or immoral behavior.
A marine fish, the cobia (Rachycentron canadum).

core.definition: A person who returns home after wasteful, reckless living and is welcomed back with forgiveness, especially after repenting of past misconduct.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SON, the main word, with a lighter secondary stress on PROD. Say the flapped t-less 'prodigal' with a clear, reduced final syllable, so it sounds like 'prah-dih-gul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or sympathetic, since the phrase celebrates forgiveness and return, though the story begins with wasteful behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for anyone who comes back after a long absence or estrangement, often with a hint of warm forgiveness. It appears in sermons, family conversation, and news stories about reconciliation. A natural reply, when someone describes a returning relative, is 'Well, it's good to have him back.'

distinctions.note: A black sheep is a family member who is disgraced or disapproved of, but the phrase does not imply a return or forgiveness as the prodigal son does.
A prodigy is a person of exceptional talent, usually young, with no link to wrongdoing or repentance.

collocations: the parable of the prodigal son

examples.everyday: My cousin finally came back to town after five years, and Mom threw a party like he was the prodigal son.
examples.professional: Our former engineer rejoined the team last month, and the manager joked that he was the prodigal son of the data group.
examples.analytical: The parable of the prodigal son invites readers to examine how the father's unconditional welcome reframes the younger son's repentance.

nuance.analogy: Like a lost sheep found and brought back into the fold, the prodigal son's homecoming turns the story from loss to celebration.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin prodigus, meaning wasteful or lavish, from prodigere, to drive forth or squander.
common_mistakes: Saying 'prodigy son' when meaning someone who returns; 'prodigy' means a talented young person.
Stressing the first word too heavily, making the phrase sound like 'PRAH-dih-gul SON' with equal emphasis.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase comes from Jesus' parable in Luke 15:11-32, which the RSV calls the parable of the lost son, and the Greek word asōtōs (loosely, in a dissolute or wasteful way) describes the younger son's life in Luke 15:13. In Luke 15:20, the father runs to embrace the son before he can finish his speech, showing that the return is met with grace. In Luke 15:32, the father tells the older brother that it was right to rejoice because the son who was lost has been found. Note that the RSV does not use the word 'prodigal' in the text; the title is a later convention.

senses.definition: Someone who protects or guards, by assignment or on their own initiative.
A headmate who primarily fronts, or otherwise protects the system, in situations where the system is at risk of psychological harm.
A device or mechanism which is designed to protect.
One who prevents interference. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
A state or other subject under international law, exercising a protectorate over another subject in international law.

A cardinal, from one of the more considerable Roman Catholic nations, who looks after the interests of his people at Rome; also, a cardinal who has the same relation to a college, religious order, etc.

core.definition: A person or thing that guards, defends or keeps something safe from harm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on TEK. The final -or is a reduced r-colored vowel, so say it as ter, not tor, and keep the r clearly audible.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests care, responsibility and safety, though a protector can also be overbearing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protector for people who guard children, property or the environment, and for things like a screen protector or a shield. In casual speech a parent might be called a protector, and the word is warm and positive. In the Bible, God is often described as a protector.

distinctions.note: A guardian has legal responsibility for someone, usually a minor; a protector may have no legal role.
A defender is someone who fights against an attack; a protector is broader and may prevent harm rather than respond to it.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was always the protector of the family, making sure everyone got home safe.
examples.professional: The security team acts as the protector of customer data, so every access request is logged.
examples.analytical: The psalmist names the LORD as his protector, a shield who guards the one who trusts in him.

nuance.analogy: A protector is like a lighthouse that stays lit through the storm so ships can find their way to safe harbor.
nuance.etymology: From Latin protector, defender, from protegere, to cover in front.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as tor instead of ter.
Confusing protector with protection, the noun for the act or the thing that protects.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, magen (מָגֵן) means shield, and it is used of God as protector. Psalm 18:2 describes the LORD as a rock, fortress, deliverer and shield in whom the psalmist takes refuge. Genesis 15:1 has God tell Abram, I am your shield. Psalm 28:7 says the LORD is the psalmist's strength and shield, in whom his heart trusts.

protector.etymology: From Middle English *protectour*, from Anglo-Norman *protectour*, *protector* and its etymon Latin *prōtēctor*, from *prōtegō* (“shield, protect”).

senses.definition: Possessing, exercising, or demonstrating great care and consideration for the future.
Showing care in the use of something (especially money or provisions), so as to avoid wasting it.
Providing (for someone’s needs).

core.definition: Careful and wise in planning for the future, especially in saving money or resources.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced 'ih', and the ending '-ent' is a quick 'unt', not 'ent' as in 'bent'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises prudent planning and thrift.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use provident mainly in formal writing, older-style speech or religious contexts. In everyday talk, people more often say 'careful,' 'prudent' or 'thrifty.' Calling a neighbor provident would sound slightly formal but complimentary.

distinctions.note: Prudent emphasizes sound judgment in choices; provident emphasizes planning and saving for future needs.
Thrifty focuses on spending little; provident focuses on preparing for what lies ahead.

examples.everyday: My uncle has always been provident with money, so he never worried about a rainy day.
examples.professional: A provident capacity plan keeps the cluster from running out of memory during the quarterly peak.
examples.analytical: A provident ethic of stewardship, as the author argues, links present restraint to the good of future generations.

nuance.analogy: Like a squirrel storing nuts before winter: it looks ahead and saves for the cold months.
nuance.etymology: From Latin providens, present participle of providere, to foresee.
common_mistakes: Confusing provident with 'prudent' in every context; provident focuses on planning ahead.
Mispronouncing it as 'PROH-vih-dent'; the first syllable is PRAH.

senses.definition: The quality of being provincial; having provincial tastes, mentality, manners.
senses.example: The blacksmith's provincialism showed in his speech and manner

senses.definition: A word or locution characteristic of a region or district.
Synonym of regionalism: belief in the superiority of one's regional government; the belief that most or nearly all political power should be decentralized to provincial governments.

core.definition: Narrowness of outlook or taste; the quality of being limited to one's local area and unaware of wider ideas or customs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, VIN. The middle vowels reduce to a weak uh, and the final -ism is a light, unstressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone provincial suggests they are unsophisticated or narrow-minded, though the word can be neutral when describing a local dialect or culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in essays, reviews and political commentary, for example to criticize a city's insularity or a politician's narrow views. In casual speech people more often say narrow-minded or small-town. Saying someone has provincialism to their face can sound harsh, so it is better kept for describing ideas or attitudes in discussion.

distinctions.note: Parochialism refers to a narrow focus on one's own small community or interests, often church or neighborhood, while provincialism is broader and stresses a lack of worldliness or sophistication.
Regionalism can be a neutral or positive term for loyalty to a region or its cultural traits; provincialism implies that the same loyalty has become narrow or dismissive.

examples.everyday: My cousin from Ohio thinks New York is weird, and honestly, that kind of provincialism gets old fast.
examples.professional: Our product team needs to fight a bit of provincialism and look at how users in Asia and Europe actually use the app.
examples.analytical: Critics have long argued that the novel's provincialism lies not in its setting but in its refusal to imagine any perspective beyond the narrator's village.

nuance.analogy: Like a house with the blinds always down, provincialism keeps out the light of the wider world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin provincialis, relating to a province, a territory administered outside Rome.
common_mistakes: Using provincialism to mean simply living in a small town; it implies narrowness, not location.
Confusing the stress, saying PROV-in-shuh-liz-um instead of pruh-VIN-shuh-liz-um.

senses.definition: Happening every day; daily.
Having the characteristics of something which can be seen, experienced, etc, every day or very commonly.
Something which is considered humdrum or dull.
Recurring every twenty-four hours or (more generally) daily (of symptoms, etc).
Commonplace or mundane things regarded as a class.
A daily allowance formerly paid to certain members of the clergy.
A fever which recurs every day; quotidian malaria.

core.definition: Happening every day; ordinary, routine, or commonplace, often in a way that seems dull.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, TID. The final "-ian" is a reduced syllable pronounced "un," not "ee-an."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting something routine that may be dull; it can also be neutral when describing ordinary life without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quotidian mainly in writing, essays, and literary criticism, not in casual conversation. Speakers who use it in everyday talk may sound pretentious, so "daily" or "everyday" is the natural choice. It works well when describing the ordinary details of life, such as chores or routines.

distinctions.note: Daily is the common everyday word, while quotidian is more literary and can carry a tone of dullness or routine.
Mundane stresses boredom and lack of interest; quotidian stresses ordinary, repeated occurrence and can be neutral.

examples.everyday: Honestly, my quotidian chores like folding laundry are the part of my day I least enjoy.
examples.professional: The team's quotidian reporting tasks can be automated so analysts focus on the harder questions.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard saw the quotidian as the very place where faith is tested, not a distraction from it.

nuance.analogy: Quotidian is like a well-worn pair of slippers: comfortable, always there, and so familiar that you stop noticing them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quotidianus, "daily," from quotidie, "every day," from quot, "how many" and dies, "day."
common_mistakes: Using quotidian as a noun in everyday speech; it is mainly an adjective.
Pronouncing the last syllable as "ee-an" instead of "un."

quotidian.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *cotidian*, *cotidien*, Middle French *cotidian*, *cotidien*, and their source, Latin *cottīdiānus*, *quōtīdiānus* (“happening every day”), from adverb *cottidie*, *quōtīdiē* (“every day, daily”), from an unattested adjective derived from…

senses.definition: To modify core data from which other data is derived in such a way that the final meaning is unchanged.
To change the base address of.
To integrate changes by appending them to another commit or branch, rather than pulling or merging in changes from a branch.
To replace the base of a denture.

core.definition: In version control, to move a branch's commits onto a different base commit, replaying them so the history reads as a straight line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BASE, the same syllable as in 'base'. Many engineers say RE-base, which is wrong, and the final s becomes /ɪz/ in 'rebases'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Git users say it as both verb and noun, as in 'let's rebase onto main' or 'do an interactive rebase'. Careful use matters: rebasing commits that others already pushed forces teammates to reconcile their histories. Outside software, the word is almost never used.

distinctions.note: A merge joins two branches with a new merge commit that keeps both histories; a rebase rewrites your commits on top of the target branch.
A reset moves a branch pointer, often to discard commits; a rebase replays existing commits onto a new base.

examples.everyday: I'm stuck in the middle of a rebase, so I can't look at the new file yet.
examples.professional: Can you rebase your feature branch onto main before we review the pull request?
examples.analytical: A rebase preserves the content of each commit while changing its parent, so the history looks linear but no longer shows when the work actually happened.

nuance.analogy: Like copying your notes from one folder onto a fresh page in a new order, so they read straight through.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' plus base, from Greek basis 'step, foundation'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (RE-base) instead of ree-BAYS.
Using rebase to mean pull or merge; a rebase replays commits and rewrites history.
Rebasing shared commits that others have already pulled, which causes confusion for teammates.

senses.definition: Something that restrains, ties, fastens or secures.
senses.example: Make sure all the restraints are tight.

senses.definition: Control or caution; reserve.
senses.example: Try to exercise restraint when talking to your boss.

core.definition: Self-control in speech or action, or a device or force that holds someone or something back.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on -STRAINT, and the final t is clear and crisp. Do not add an extra vowel before the t, and keep the first syllable short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: positive when it means self-control, negative or neutral when it means a physical device or legal limit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans praise a person for showing restraint, meaning they did not overreact or overeat or spend too much. The word also appears in police and medical settings, as in physical restraints. In casual talk, you might say 'I showed a lot of restraint,' and a friend may laugh and agree.

distinctions.note: Self-control is a broad quality, while restraint often describes holding back in a particular moment, such as not speaking or not spending.
Restriction is an external rule or limit, while restraint usually comes from a person's own choice or a device used to hold someone.

examples.everyday: She showed real restraint and did not argue with the waiter.
examples.professional: I appreciate your restraint during the escalation; it kept the client calm.
examples.analytical: Virtue ethics treats restraint not as repression but as the disciplined ordering of desire toward the good.

nuance.analogy: Like a brake that lets a car descend a hill safely.
nuance.etymology: From Old French restrainte, from restreindre, to restrain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun restraint with the verb restrain, which takes no noun ending.
Mispronouncing the final t as silent or adding an extra vowel.

restraint.etymology: From Middle English *restreynte*, from Old French *restreinte*; more at *restrain*.

core.definition: The name of Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian, in the book of Exodus.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, ROO, and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'ROO-ul'. Keep the r clear at the start.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a biblical name without strong emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet the name Reuel in Bible study. In Exodus the same man is also called Jethro, so readers sometimes need to know that they are the same person.

examples.everyday: In Bible study we noticed that Reuel and Jethro seem to be the same man in Exodus.
examples.professional: In my sermon on Exodus 2, I explained that Reuel welcomed Moses into his household after his flight to Midian.
examples.analytical: The narrative's naming of Reuel as a priest of Midian shows that the Israelite story recognizes a wider religious context outside Israel.

nuance.analogy: Like a host whose name appears in two different places in the same story.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Re'uel, often understood as 'friend of God' or 'friend of El'.
common_mistakes: Assuming Reuel and Jethro are different people; in Exodus they appear to be the same figure under two names.
Saying 'REE-ool' instead of 'ROO-ul'.
nuance.biblical_note: Reuel (Re'u'el, רְעוּאֵל) is the name of the priest of Midian who was the father-in-law of Moses. Exodus 2:18 gives his name as Reuel when Moses comes to his household after fleeing Egypt. Numbers 10:29 mentions 'Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite' as Moses' brother-in-law, showing the family connection. Exodus 3:1 and 18:1 call the same man Jethro, which many scholars take to be a second name or a title.

senses.definition: A setting that controls how random a model's output is: lower is more predictable, higher is more varied.

core.definition: In AI, a setting that controls how random a language model's output is: lower values give more predictable text, higher values more varied text.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrase, the main stress moves to temperature; the first word, sampling, gets a secondary stress. Say temp as TEM and the final syllable as a reduced r-colored vowel, not tuh or tyoor.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Developers and data scientists use sampling temperature when configuring models through APIs or libraries. In a meeting, Americans say 'let's lower the temperature' or 'set the temp to 0.2' informally. The term is technical, so explain it briefly when speaking with non-specialists.

distinctions.note: Top-p (nucleus sampling) limits choices to a cumulative probability mass, while temperature rescales the whole probability distribution.
Temperature alone is the physical measure of heat, while sampling temperature is a model setting for randomness.

examples.everyday: My chatbot sounds too random, so I'm going to turn the sampling temperature down.
examples.professional: For the extraction pipeline, we set the sampling temperature to zero so the outputs are reproducible across runs.
examples.analytical: Raising the sampling temperature flattens the softmax distribution, which increases entropy and diversity but also the chance of incoherent tokens.

nuance.analogy: Sampling temperature is like a dial on a radio: turned down, the station is clear and predictable; turned up, it gets noisy and surprising.
nuance.etymology: Sampling from sample (verb); temperature from Latin temperatura, a mixing or proper measure.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing temperature with four clear syllables instead of three, with the middle one reduced.
Confusing sampling temperature with the physical temperature of the server or room.

conversation.text: Sampling temperature divides the logits before the softmax; lower values sharpen the distribution and higher values flatten it.
Set the sampling temperature to zero for extraction tasks; we want consistency, not creativity.
Sampling temperature is like a creativity dial: low is predictable, high is more surprising and more error-prone.

senses.definition: One who scans.
A device which scans documents in order to convert them to a digital medium.
senses.example: He put the picture in the scanner, then e-mailed a copy of it to his family.

senses.definition: A device which scans barcodes or QR codes for the purpose of charging a customer, performing a price check or enquiry, printing a price label or sticker, checking an item in or out of the store or warehouse, or finding an item ordered through click and collect and its corresponding location; a pricing gun or HHT.
A radio receiver which iterates through a sequence of frequencies to detect signal.
A device which uses radiation (ultrasound, X-ray, etc.) to generate images of tissue or surfaces for diagnostic purposes.
A device which uses optics to detect printed data (such as a barcode).

core.definition: A device that reads barcodes, QR codes or paper documents and converts them into digital information.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKAN. The final -er is a reduced American 'er', not 'ahr'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scanner for the barcode reader at a store checkout, the flatbed scanner at an office, and the handheld price-check device the staff uses on shelves. People say 'the scanner beeped' or 'the cashier scanned my items.' A handheld device used to print price labels is usually called a pricing gun.

distinctions.note: A copier makes a paper duplicate of a document; a scanner converts it into a digital file.
Reader is a general term; scanner usually refers to a device that captures an image or barcode in one pass.

examples.everyday: The cashier's scanner beeped twice, so I know the discount came through.
examples.professional: Can you scan the signed contract on the office scanner and send it as a PDF?
examples.analytical: A scanner converts analog documents into digital data, which raises questions about accuracy and metadata.

nuance.analogy: A scanner is like a camera that photographs paper and turns the picture into a computer file.
nuance.etymology: From scan, which comes from Latin scandere, to climb, a term later used for scanning verse.
common_mistakes: Using scanner for a camera; a scanner converts documents or codes into digital data.
Putting the stress on the second syllable, as in 'skan-AIR'.

conversation.text: The scanner isn't reading the coupon on my phone.
There's a price scanner in aisle five if you want to check a price.
The cashier passed each item over the scanner really fast.

senses.definition: A former Hebrew unit of dry volume, about 7.7 L or 7 quarts.

core.definition: An ancient Hebrew unit of dry measure, about seven quarts or 7.7 liters, used for grain and flour.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak schwa. Do not pronounce it as sea-ah with two full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized term from biblical studies and archaeology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly meet seah in Bible study, commentaries, and archaeology texts. Most English Bibles, including the RSV, translate it as measure, so in church you may hear measure of meal more often. Use seah only when you discuss the Hebrew term directly.

distinctions.note: An ephah was a larger dry measure, about ten times a seah, so the two are not interchangeable.
An omer was a smaller measure used for daily manna, while a seah was a larger quantity of grain or flour.

examples.everyday: The Bible study leader said the old word measure in that verse was really a seah.
examples.professional: Our Hebrew translation notes list the seah as roughly seven quarts for dry goods.
examples.analytical: The seah in Genesis 18:6 signals a generous offering of flour, which shows the hospitality Abraham extends to his guests.

nuance.analogy: A seah is like an old family cookie-jar measure, a traditional container size that has a precise value only to those who know the custom.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew se'ah, a unit of dry measure.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as sea-uh with two equal syllables.
Assuming it is the same as an ephah, which was a larger unit.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word se'ah (סְאָה) denotes a dry measure, about a third of an ephah. The RSV usually renders it as measure, so readers should check the Hebrew for the exact quantity. Genesis 18:6 describes Sarah preparing three measures of fine meal for the visitors, and 2 Kings 7:1 mentions a measure of fine flour sold for a shekel during the siege of Samaria. The unit's size shows that these texts speak of ordinary abundance and provision.

senses.definition: A type of fabric made from the skin of seals.
Any fabric manufactured to resemble sealskin.
An item of clothing made from sealskin (whether real or imitation).

core.definition: Leather or fabric made from the skin of a seal, or an imitation of it used for clothing and bags.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second word is a short i. Seal and sealskin both keep the long ee sound, so do not shorten it to sell.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It can evoke luxury, but many people now object to seal products on ethical grounds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sealskin for the material and sealskin coat for clothing, which is considered luxury wear in some circles. Many people now avoid it for animal welfare reasons, and in the US the import and sale of seal products is restricted. In everyday talk, faux sealskin may be mentioned to describe imitation fabric.

distinctions.note: Fur refers to animal hair with the pelt, while sealskin usually refers to the leather or pelt itself.
Leather is tanned hide in general, while sealskin specifically means skin from seals.

examples.everyday: My aunt still has her old sealskin coat from the 1960s, but she doesn't wear it anymore.
examples.professional: The fashion buyer asked whether our supplier could provide a faux sealskin alternative for the winter line.
examples.analytical: The sealskin coat became a symbol of status and of the ethical debates surrounding animal products in modern consumer culture.

nuance.analogy: Sealskin is like a heavy wool blanket for the body, a material people once prized for warmth but now question because of how it is made.
nuance.etymology: Compound of seal (the animal) and skin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing seal as sell, which makes the word unclear.
Assuming sealskin and seal leather are different materials, when they are the same kind of skin in different forms.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew tachash (תַּחַשׁ) in the tabernacle instructions has an uncertain meaning, and translations vary between badger skins and other hides. The RSV renders it as badger skins, so readers should not assume a direct biblical reference to sealskin. Exodus 25:5 and Exodus 26:14 list such skins among the materials for the tabernacle, which shows the desert community's use of durable animal hides.

senses.definition: Each of the divisions of a year based on the prevailing weather: spring, summer, autumn (fall) and winter; or the rainy (monsoon) and dry season, depending on the climate.
A period of the year when something particular happens.
senses.example: mating season

senses.definition: A period of the year in which a place is most busy or frequented for business, amusement, etc.
A year, but with emphasis on the most important part of the year in context, such as the months when plants or animals grow and reproduce.
senses.example: This invasive species reproduces so rapidly that it can completely take over an area in just a couple seasons.

senses.definition: A period of time in one’s life characterized by a particular emotion of situation.
senses.example: a season of faithlessness

senses.definition: A fixed period of time in a massively multiplayer online game in which new content (themes, rules, modes, etc.) becomes available, sometimes replacing earlier content.
The period over which a series of Test matches are played.
The full set of downloadable content for a game, which can be purchased with a season pass.
To flavor food with spices, herbs or salt.
To habituate, accustom, or inure (someone or something) to a particular use, purpose, or circumstance.
senses.example: to season oneself to a climate

senses.definition: To prepare by drying or hardening, or removal of natural juices.
senses.example: The timber needs to be seasoned.

senses.definition: To become mature; to grow fit for use; to become adapted to a climate.
To become dry and hard, by the escape of the natural juices, or by being penetrated with other substance.
senses.example: The wood has seasoned in the sun.

senses.definition: To mingle: to moderate, temper, or qualify by admixture.

core.definition: One of the four periods of the year, spring, summer, fall or winter, each defined by its typical weather.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced schwa followed by a syllabic n, so it sounds like one syllable ending in n, not two separate vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is used for everyday time references and sports talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the four seasons or in the summer season for weather, and also use season for sports, TV, and shopping periods. In American English the fall is the usual word for autumn, though autumn appears in formal writing. For the rainy or dry period in tropical places, season is also common.

distinctions.note: Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions, while season is a longer period of the year defined by typical weather patterns.
Time is a general concept, while season specifically marks a recurring period of the year.

examples.everyday: I love this time of year, it is my favorite season, with the leaves turning and the cool air.
examples.professional: Our sales spike every season, so we staff up for the holiday rush in November.
examples.analytical: The ancient calendar divided the year into agricultural seasons, linking human labor to recurring natural cycles.

nuance.analogy: A season is like a chapter in the year's book, each with its own weather, mood and purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Old French seison, from Latin satio, meaning sowing, the time for planting.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full vowel instead of a syllabic n.
Using season for a single day; a season is a longer period.

season.etymology: From Middle English *sesoun* (“time of the year”), from Old French *seson* (“time of sowing, seeding”), from Latin *satiō* (“act of sowing, planting”) from *satum*, past participle of *serō* (“to sow, plant”) from Proto-Indo-European **seh₁-* (“to sow,…

conversation.text: Season the chicken with salt and pepper.
I seasoned the fries with garlic salt.
Tomatoes taste best in summer when they're in season.
It's been a rough season for the Bears.
Baseball season starts in the spring.
Have you watched the new season yet?
Fall is my favorite season; I love the colors.

core.definition: King of Assyria (705–681 BC) who invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem during the reign of King Hezekiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAK, the second syllable. The middle syllables are reduced to schwas, and the final -rib rhymes with 'rib'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use; in Bible study it stands for a threatening enemy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually meet this name in Bible study, church reading, history classes or sermons. In casual talk you would rarely use it; you might say 'the Assyrian king' instead. If someone asks who he was, a natural answer is 'the Assyrian king who attacked Jerusalem in the Bible'.

distinctions.note: Nebuchadnezzar was the Babylonian king who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC; Sennacherib was an Assyrian king who besieged it about a century earlier.
Sargon II was Sennacherib's father, an Assyrian king who conquered Samaria in 722 BC.

examples.everyday: Did you know Sennacherib's army once surrounded Jerusalem in the Bible?
examples.professional: In our Isaiah sermon series, we will look at how Sennacherib's threat shapes Hezekiah's prayer.
examples.analytical: Isaiah presents Sennacherib's boasting as a foil to the LORD's sovereignty, a contrast that structures the narrative of chapters 36 to 37.

nuance.analogy: Like a bully who threatens a small town, only to be stopped by someone far stronger than the town's walls.
nuance.etymology: From Akkadian Sîn-aḫḫē-erība, usually read as 'Sin has replaced the brothers'; the Hebrew form Sanḥērîb follows the same pattern.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first or last syllable; the stress falls on NAK.
Confusing him with other Assyrian or Babylonian kings, such as Nebuchadnezzar or Sargon.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew name: Sanḥērîḇ (סַנְחֵרִיב), the Hebrew form of the Assyrian king's name. Key passages: 2 Kings 18:13 describes his invasion of Judah and capture of the fortified cities. 2 Kings 19:35 tells how the angel of the LORD strikes down the Assyrian camp in one night, and 2 Kings 19:36 to 37 describes his return to Nineveh and his murder by his own sons. Isaiah 36 to 37 tells the same story from Isaiah's perspective, and 2 Chronicles 32 gives a parallel account.

senses.definition: A separate bill for each person or couple at the table.

core.definition: Separate bills for each person or couple at a restaurant table, so each pays only for their own order.

pronunciation.tip: In the adjective separate, stress the first syllable and reduce the middle to 'uh', so it sounds like SEP-rit. The word checks is often said quickly with a clear ch sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, polite request in restaurants.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, you can ask for separate checks at a restaurant, and servers hear this often. You can also say can we split the check or we'd like separate checks, depending on the situation. The word check is used for the bill in American English, while bill is more common in British English.

distinctions.note: Split the check means dividing one bill among the group. Separate checks means each person gets their own bill.
The bill is common in British English for the restaurant total. Americans say the check.

examples.everyday: Could we get separate checks, please? I only had a salad and water.
examples.professional: After the client lunch, I asked the server for separate checks so expenses could be filed correctly.
examples.analytical: Restaurants often prefer separate checks because they make tipping and tax tracking simpler for each diner.

nuance.analogy: Separate checks are like giving each guest their own receipt at a shared meal, even though they ate at the same table.
common_mistakes: Saying separated checks instead of separate checks.
Saying the bill when Americans usually say the check.

conversation.text: Can we get separate checks, please? We'll each pay for our own.
Sorry, we can't do separate checks for parties over eight.
Let the server know now if you want separate checks.

senses.definition: The cardinal number immediately following seventy-six and preceding seventy-eight.

core.definition: The cardinal number 77, one more than seventy-six and one less than seventy-eight.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, SEV-en, and keep the first word lighter. The final syllable of seven is a reduced schwa-n sound, so do not add an extra vowel after the n.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a number word with no emotional charge, though in Scripture it carries symbolic weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say seventy-seven for the number in counting, addresses, scores, and prices. In casual speech people may say seventy-seven without the hyphen when reading numbers aloud, but the written form keeps the hyphen. The figure 77 is common in writing.

distinctions.note: Seventy-seven is a cardinal; seventy-seventh is the ordinal used for position 77.
Seven times seventy is an arithmetic description, while seventy-seven is the standard name for the number.

examples.everyday: The hotel room is seventy-seven, right at the end of the hall.
examples.professional: Our test set has seventy-seven failing cases, and we are down to nine after the patch.
examples.analytical: Jesus answers Peter that forgiveness must be given seventy-seven times, which Matthew presents as an open-ended limit rather than an exact count.

nuance.analogy: Like a double lucky seven: the same digit repeated, which makes it easy to remember.
nuance.etymology: Formed from seventy plus seven, from Old English seofontig and seofon.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable SEV-en-tee instead of the second.
Writing seventy seven without a hyphen in formal writing.
nuance.biblical_note: Seventy-seven appears in Genesis 4:24 in the RSV, where Lamech boasts of avenging himself seventy-sevenfold. In Matthew 18:22 Jesus tells Peter to forgive seventy-seven times, which contrasts with Peter's proposal of seven times, pointing to unlimited forgiveness.

senses.definition: A software component that runs in a separate process from the rest of the software, to provide isolation and encapsulation.
A one-wheeled attachment to the side of a motorcycle to allow for a separate seat for a passenger or cargo space.
A cocktail made with cognac (or brandy), triple sec liqueur, and lemon juice.

core.definition: A small car-like attachment on the side of a motorcycle, with its own seat for a passenger.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable car has a clear rhotic r, and the vowel is the open American ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a fairly specialized word, and its meaning in software or cocktail contexts is quite different.
nuance.usage_note: In American English the word mainly describes a motorcycle attachment, often in recreational riding or vintage motorcycle talk. Software engineers use it for a separate helper process, and bartenders use it for a cognac cocktail. Always clarify the context if you use it at work.

distinctions.note: A trailer is towed behind a vehicle, while a sidecar is attached to the side of a motorcycle.
A sidewalk is a footpath for pedestrians, and sidecar is a motorcycle attachment, so the words are unrelated despite the shared side.

examples.everyday: My uncle took the whole family out on his old motorcycle with a sidecar.
examples.professional: We run the monitoring agent as a sidecar process so it can be updated without touching the main service.
examples.analytical: The sidecar pattern separates auxiliary functions from the core application, much as the attachment separates the passenger's seat from the motorcycle's engine.

nuance.analogy: A sidecar is like a second seat strapped onto a bicycle, giving a passenger their own space while the main vehicle does the driving.
nuance.etymology: From side and car, describing a car-like attachment at the side of a motorcycle.
common_mistakes: Using sidecar for a trailer or a towed cart; the word refers to the attachment on a motorcycle.
Assuming the software sense is common in everyday American talk; it is specialized.

senses.definition: To cause to be seated or in a sitting posture; to furnish a seat to.
senses.example: Sit your ass down and shut up.

senses.definition: To assume a sitting position from a standing position.
senses.example: Sit down! We have work to do.

senses.definition: To meet formally at a conference table.
To meet with someone for discussions, negotiations or interrogation.
senses.example: I sat down with him about the allegations.

senses.definition: To assume a low or sunken position.
senses.example: The ball scooted off the fairway and sat down in the thick rough.

senses.definition: In Aboriginal use, to live or stay at (a place).

core.definition: To lower your body into a chair or other seat, or to ask someone to take a seat.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DOWN, and the t in 'sit' is flapped and quick, so it sounds close to 'si-DOWN'. In fast speech the phrase links to sound like 'si-DOWN'.

nuance.connotation: positive or neutral; it is a polite and friendly invitation or instruction, but a sharp 'Sit down!' can sound bossy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Have a seat' or 'Please, sit down' when welcoming a guest, and 'Sit down' is common with children or pets. For a serious talk, Americans might say 'We need to sit down and talk.' The word 'sit' alone is not used for a seated guest in the same way, so the phrasal verb is standard.

distinctions.note: Sit down focuses on the act of moving from standing to seated, while sit can refer to simply being in a seat.
Take a seat is a polite, slightly more formal invitation, whereas sit down is more direct and common in casual speech.

examples.everyday: Come on in and sit down, the coffee's almost ready.
examples.professional: Let's sit down together after the stand-up and go over the dashboard numbers.
examples.analytical: Socrates asks his students to sit down and examine their assumptions before they claim to know what justice is.

nuance.analogy: It is like taking a chair at a table you were invited to join: you move from standing to settled.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sittan (to sit) and the adverb down, meaning to lower oneself to a lower position.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sit' alone to invite someone to take a chair in a casual setting, which sounds unnatural. Use 'sit down' or 'have a seat'.
Pronouncing the t in 'sit' as a hard, full t, when American speech usually flaps it in connected speech.

conversation.text: Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.
We need to sit down and talk about our budget.

senses.definition: To explain in clear and simple terms; to be explicit.
senses.example: Here is a brochure that spells out the benefits.

senses.definition: To form (a word) from letters; say the letters in a word.
senses.example: He used Scrabble tiles to spell out “I LOVE YOU”.

senses.definition: To replace an abbreviation with its unabbreviated form, such an acronym with its expansion.
senses.example: To avoid crypticness for nonexpert readers, she spelled out the phrase, so that "tips about PrEP in the context of OHS for HCPs" became "tips about preexposure prophylaxis in the context of occupational health and safety for health care professionals".

core.definition: To explain something clearly and in detail so that nothing is left unclear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OUT, the second word, which is the main stress of the phrase. Say 'spel-OUT' with a clear, strong ow sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests clarity and careful communication.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spell out constantly at work and in everyday talk, as in 'Can you spell that out for me?' It is polite and useful when you want someone to slow down and explain. It can also mean saying the letters of a word aloud, which is common on the phone.

distinctions.note: Explain is broad and can be formal; spell out suggests going through every detail step by step, often when the listener has not understood.
Clarify means to make something clearer; spell out implies giving every explicit detail, sometimes more than needed.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I didn't follow the directions, can you spell them out for me one more time?
examples.professional: Can you spell out the timeline for the migration in the next meeting so the whole team knows the dependencies?
examples.analytical: The theologian spells out the implications of grace for human agency, showing how each premise leads to the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Spelling out an idea is like unfolding a map step by step, so the traveler sees every turn before setting out.
nuance.etymology: 'Spell' from Old English 'spellian' meaning to tell or relate, combined with 'out'.
common_mistakes: Putting a pronoun after the particle incorrectly; say 'spell it out', not 'spell out it'.
Confusing the explain sense with the say-the-letters sense; context usually shows which is meant.

conversation.text: Do I have to spell it out for you? I'm not interested.
The contract spells out exactly what we're responsible for.
Could you spell out your last name for me?
Can you spell out exactly what you need from us?
The contract spells out the payment terms.
Let me spell it out: we can't launch without legal approval.

senses.definition: To drop something so that it spreads out or makes a mess; to accidentally pour.
senses.example: I spilled some sticky juice on the kitchen floor.

senses.definition: To spread out or fall out, as above.
senses.example: Some sticky juice spilled onto the kitchen floor.

senses.definition: To overflow out of a designated area.
senses.example: The crowd spilled onto Maple Avenue.

senses.definition: To drop something that was intended to be caught.
To mar; to damage; to destroy by misuse; to waste.
To overflow or flow out, over or off something.
To cause or flow out and be lost or wasted; to shed.
To cover or decorate with slender pieces of wood, metal, ivory, etc. to inlay.
To reveal information to an uninformed party.
senses.example: He spilled his guts out to his new psychologist.

senses.definition: To come undone.
To express (something), especially repeatedly or floridly; to be expressed.
senses.example: He spilled insults about the other team.

senses.definition: To relieve a sail from the pressure of the wind, so that it can be more easily reefed or furled, or to lessen the strain.
Any thing that has been spilled; the resulting mess.
A fall or stumble.
senses.example: The bruise is from a bad spill he had last week.

senses.definition: Synonym of taper, a thin stick, long wick, etc. used to transfer flame.
A slender piece of anything. A spillikin.
A peg or pin for plugging a hole, as in a cask'; a spile.
A metallic rod or pin.
A spillikin.
A splinter caught in the skin.
One of the thick laths or poles driven horizontally ahead of the main timbering in advancing a level in loose ground.
The situation where sound is picked up by a microphone from a source other than that which is intended.

core.definition: To let liquid or loose material fall or flow out of a container, often by accident.

pronunciation.tip: The word has one syllable with a short i, like 'sit' and 'fill'. The l is clear, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: neutral to slightly negative when accidental; the word suggests a mess that needs cleaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Oops, I spilled it' when they knock over a drink, and 'spill' is also used for oil or chemicals leaking. In a restaurant, a server might say they will get a towel for a spill. The past tense can be 'spilled' or 'spilt', but 'spilled' is much more common in American English.

distinctions.note: Pour means to deliberately flow liquid from a container, while spill means to flow out by accident.
Leak usually means a slow escape through a crack or hole, while spill is a quicker or larger release, often on a surface.

examples.everyday: Careful, you're going to spill your coffee if you keep walking with it like that.
examples.professional: The facilities team cleaned up the chemical spill in the lab within an hour.
examples.analytical: The metaphor of spilled water suggests that once experience has been poured out, it cannot be restored to its original container.

nuance.analogy: A spill is like a glass tipped over on a table: the liquid escapes and spreads everywhere.
nuance.etymology: From Old English spillan, meaning to destroy or waste.
common_mistakes: Using 'spill' to mean a deliberate pouring, such as pouring soup into a bowl.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long ee, as in 'speel'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 38:9, the Hebrew verb shachat (שָׁחַת), meaning to spoil or destroy, is rendered as 'spilled' in the RSV, describing Onan's wasteful act. The passage shows how the English word translates a stronger idea of ruin than a simple accident.

spill.etymology: From Middle English *spillen*, from Old English *spillan*, *spildan* (“to kill, destroy, waste”), from **spilþijan*, from Proto-Germanic **spilþijaną* (“to spoil, kill, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European **pel-* (“to sunder, split, rend, tear”).

senses.definition: Any of a number of smooth curves used to join points.
A long, thin piece of metal or wood.
A strip of wood or other material inserted into grooves in each of two pieces of wood to provide additional surface for gluing.
A flexible strip of metal or other material, that may be bent into a curve and used in a similar manner to a ruler to draw smooth curves between points.

A ridge or tooth on a drive shaft that meshes with a corresponding groove in a mating piece and transfers torque to it, maintaining the angular correspondence between the pieces; either the ridge or the groove, as part of a set of both (splines); the whole set of ridges and grooves.
A rectangular piece that fits grooves like key seats in a hub and a shaft, so that while the one may slide endwise on the other, both must revolve together.
To smooth (a curve or surface) by means of a spline.
To fit with a spline.
To fasten to or together with a spline.

core.definition: A smooth piecewise polynomial curve used to join or fit a set of data points or control points.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a diphthong that starts open and glides toward i. Do not add a vowel between the s and the p.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used in precise professional contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spline mainly in mathematics, computer graphics, engineering, and data analysis. It is a technical word, so in general conversation people would not use it. The verb sense means to fit or smooth a curve using splines.

distinctions.note: Curve is a general word for any bent line; a spline is a specific kind of piecewise polynomial curve.
A polynomial is a single algebraic expression; a spline joins several polynomial pieces with smooth connections.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law builds furniture, and he used a spline to join two pieces of wood.
examples.professional: We used a cubic spline to smooth the sensor readings before feeding them into the model.
examples.analytical: A spline interpolant minimizes curvature among smooth functions that pass through the given data points.

nuance.analogy: Like a flexible wooden drafting strip bent through pins, it passes smoothly through each point.
nuance.etymology: Possibly from a Middle English or Dutch word for a thin strip of wood or metal; the mathematical sense comes from the flexible drafting strip.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word as splinter or spline with extra syllables.
Using spline as a general word for any curve, which is too narrow.

senses.definition: Divide the bill so each person pays for their own share.

core.definition: Divide a restaurant bill so that each person pays their own share or an equal amount.

pronunciation.tip: The word the reduces to a quick uh sound before a consonant, so say thuh. Check is the main stress, and the ch is one sound, not two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It sounds friendly and casual, and it is standard in American restaurant culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say split the check when a group wants to pay separately or equally. Check means the bill in American restaurants. A natural reply is Sure, let's split it or Can we get separate checks, please? Splitting is common among friends, but some people prefer to pay exactly what they ordered.

distinctions.note: Split the bill is also common and means the same thing; check is the American word for the restaurant bill.
Go Dutch means each person pays for themselves, but it is often used for dates or informal meals rather than a group bill.

examples.everyday: The food was great, so let's just split the check four ways and be done with it.
examples.professional: After the team lunch, we split the check so that the expense reports stayed clean.
examples.analytical: The custom of splitting the check reveals how small groups negotiate fairness in shared consumption.

nuance.analogy: Like cutting a pizza into equal slices, the total is divided among everyone at the table.
nuance.etymology: Split comes from Middle English splitten; check in this sense comes from the American restaurant bill, a slip checked against the order.
common_mistakes: Saying divide the check, which sounds unnatural; split is the usual verb.
Using bill for the American check in a formal sense without knowing that both are common.

conversation.text: Do you want to split the check, or should I just pay?
We always split the check down the middle when we go out.
Is it okay if we split the check four ways?

senses.definition: Prolonged high inflation accompanied by stagnant growth, often with recession and high unemployment.

core.definition: Economic condition of high inflation combined with slow economic growth and high unemployment at the same time.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the FLAY syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on STAG. Americans often blur the middle vowel, so say it as two strong beats with a quick, reduced ending.

nuance.connotation: negative: it names a painful economic problem, usually discussed in news, politics and policy debates.
nuance.usage_note: Economists, journalists and business leaders use stagflation mainly when discussing the 1970s or a current economic slump. Americans might say that the economy is in a bad spot with prices rising and jobs disappearing, but stagflation is the precise term. It is not used for a single bad quarter.

distinctions.note: A recession is a general fall in economic activity; stagflation is a recession or weak growth combined with high inflation, which is the unusual part.
Inflation alone means rising prices; stagflation adds stagnant growth and unemployment.

examples.everyday: My uncle says prices keep rising while his company is laying people off, and he thinks we're heading into stagflation.
examples.professional: If interest rates stay high while hiring slows, our forecast model shows a real risk of stagflation next year.
examples.analytical: Stagflation challenges the Phillips curve, since standard theory expects inflation and unemployment to move in opposite directions.

nuance.analogy: Like a car with the gas pedal pressed down while the brakes are also on: the engine works hard but the car barely moves.
nuance.etymology: Blend of stagnation and inflation, coined in the 1960s or early 1970s.
common_mistakes: Saying stagflation for any bad economy; it specifically requires both high inflation and stagnant growth.
Stressing the wrong syllable as stag-fla-TION.

stagflation.etymology: *stagnation* + *inflation*, generally thought to have been (1913–1970) in a 17 November 1965 parliamentary speech: see the quotation.

senses.definition: A conventional, formulaic, and often oversimplified or exaggerated conception, opinion, or image of (a person or a group of people).
senses.example: Not all Zumbetonians wear plimsolls. That's just a stereotype.

senses.definition: A person who is regarded as embodying or conforming to a set image or type.
An extensibility mechanism of the Unified Modeling Language, allowing a new element to be derived from an existing one with added specializations.
A metal printing plate cast from a matrix moulded from a raised printing surface.
To make a stereotype of someone or something, or characterize someone by a stereotype.
To prepare for printing in stereotype; to produce stereotype plates of.
senses.example: to stereotype the Bible

senses.definition: To print from a stereotype.
To make firm or permanent; to fix.
Of an edition: printed in stereotype.
Synonym of stereotyped.

core.definition: A widely held but oversimplified belief about what all members of a group are like.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle syllables to a quick 'ee-uh'. Keep the r clear and American, and do not say 'stair-oh-type'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes a simplified and often unfair image of a group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the word for harmful generalizations about race, gender, religion, or profession, and often say 'that's a stereotype' to challenge a remark. In casual talk it can also mean a basic image, such as the cowboy stereotype. Pointing out stereotypes can sound preachy in some settings, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Prejudice is an attitude or feeling toward a group; a stereotype is a belief about what the group is like.
A cliché is a worn-out phrase or idea; a stereotype is a fixed image of a group of people.
A generalization can be accurate and broad; a stereotype is usually oversimplified and often inaccurate.

examples.everyday: Don't buy into the stereotype that everyone from Texas wears a cowboy hat.
examples.professional: The hiring panel relied on a stereotype about older workers, so we revised the screening criteria.
examples.analytical: Stereotypes persist not only because they are false but because they replace complex social realities with quick and reassuring judgments.

nuance.analogy: A stereotype is like a caricature that exaggerates a few features until the real face disappears.
nuance.etymology: From Greek stereos (solid or firm) plus typos (impression or type); originally a printing plate cast from set type.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'sterotype' by dropping the first e.
Calling any accurate generalization a stereotype; a stereotype is specifically an oversimplified or exaggerated image.

senses.definition: Having a hardness and severity of nature or manner.
senses.example: stern sex

senses.definition: Grim and forbidding in appearance.
senses.example: The remark earned me a stern rebuke.

senses.definition: The post of management or direction.
The hinder part of anything.
The tail of an animal; now used only of the tail of a dog.
A bird, the black tern, seabird.
The rear part (after end) of a ship or other vessel.
To propel or move backward or stern-first in the water.

core.definition: Serious and strict, often in a way that makes people obey or feel nervous.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable with the r-colored vowel, like 'turn'. The t at the start is a clear t, not a flap, because it begins the word.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It suggests harsh seriousness that may feel cold, though it can be respectful in parenting or leadership.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stern for a strict parent, teacher, or boss, and for a serious facial expression. It is a description rather than a criticism, and 'a stern look' usually works as a warning. It sounds more formal or literary than strict in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Strict focuses on enforcing rules; stern focuses on a serious and forbidding manner.
Severe describes harsh punishments, conditions, or criticism; stern describes a person's manner or expression.
Firm can be positive and calm; stern is harsher and more forbidding.

examples.everyday: My grandmother gave me a stern look when I put my feet on the couch.
examples.professional: The director sent a stern email to the whole team about the missed deadlines.
examples.analytical: Stern moral teaching can convey seriousness, but without warmth it often produces fear instead of repentance.

nuance.analogy: Like a granite wall, solid and serious, with no sign of give.
nuance.etymology: From Old English, meaning severe or harsh.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adjective stern with the noun stern, meaning the back of a boat; context usually makes the difference clear.
Pronouncing it with a diphthong like 'stairn' instead of the r-colored vowel in 'turn'.

stern.etymology: From Middle English *stern*, *sterne*, *sturne*, from Old English *styrne* (“stern, grave, strict, austere, hard, severe, cruel”), from Proto-Germanic **sturnijaz* (“angry, astonished, shocked”), from Proto-Indo-European **ster-* (“rigid, stiff”).

senses.definition: Effort; the act of one who strives.

core.definition: Effort or hard work directed toward a goal, often continuous and determined.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'i' is a long 'i' like 'pie'. The second syllable is short and unstressed, and the 'ng' ending is one sound.

nuance.connotation: positive. It describes earnest effort, although in the Bible it can also describe vain effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use striving mainly in writing, speeches, and sermons about ambition or faith. In casual talk people say 'effort' or 'hard work.' The noun is less common than the verb, but it fits well in phrases like 'a life of striving'. In religious contexts, it can suggest effort to earn approval, which some Protestants see as a contrast to grace.

distinctions.note: Effort is the general, everyday word for work or energy spent. Striving suggests a deeper, more sustained or determined effort toward a goal.
Struggle often implies difficulty or hardship. Striving is more neutral and can be positive.

examples.everyday: Her years of striving finally paid off when she got the promotion.
examples.professional: The team's constant striving for better performance has improved our product quality.
examples.analytical: Ecclesiastes describes human striving after wind, the futile effort to find meaning under the sun.

nuance.analogy: Striving is like rowing upstream: the effort is constant, and progress depends on steady pulling.
nuance.etymology: From strive plus the noun suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Confusing striving with strife, which means conflict.
Using striving as a count noun with 'a striving' without context; it is usually uncountable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Ecclesiastes 1:14 in the RSV, the Preacher says all is vanity and a striving after wind. The Hebrew phrase re'ut ruach (רְעוּת רוּחַ) means a feeding on wind, a pursuit of something that cannot be grasped. Ecclesiastes 4:4 in the RSV describes toil and skill as coming from rivalry with one's neighbor, which shows the restless effort that the author sees as empty.

senses.definition: To call people together; to convene; to convoke.
To ask someone to come; to send for.
To order (goods) and have delivered.
To rouse oneself to exert a skill.
To call a resource by magic.
To summons; convene.
A creature magically summoned to do the summoner's bidding.
Call, command, order (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: To order or ask someone to come to a place, or to call people together formally.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUM. The second syllable is a weak, unstressed 'un', so don't pronounce it as a full 'mon'.

nuance.connotation: neutral to negative: it often implies authority or an order, such as a court summons.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, people say 'call', 'send for', or 'ask to come'. 'Summon' is common in legal contexts, such as a jury summons or a court summons. It can sound dramatic or stiff in casual talk, so use it for formal orders or literary effect.

distinctions.note: 'Call' is the everyday word; 'summon' is more formal and implies authority or urgency.
An invitation is polite and optional; to summon someone is to order them to come.

examples.everyday: I'll summon a taxi on my phone, so we don't have to wait in the rain.
examples.professional: The director summoned the team to a review meeting on Monday morning.
examples.analytical: In the Gospel, Jesus summons the disciples to follow him, and the call reveals their new vocation.

nuance.analogy: Like ringing a bell so that everyone in the house must come to the table.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'somondre', from Latin 'summonere', to give a hint or admonish, from 'sub' (under) and 'monere' (to warn).
common_mistakes: Using 'summon' for casual requests; 'call' or 'ask to come' sounds more natural.
Confusing 'summon' (verb) with 'summons' (noun), which is the legal document.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind 'summon' is qara' (to call, summon), and the Greek is kaleo (to call, invite). Genesis 3:9 (RSV) describes God calling to Adam after the fall, showing a personal summons. Matthew 22:3 (RSV) tells of servants sent to call those who were invited to the wedding feast. Hebrews 9:15 speaks of those who are called to receive the promised eternal inheritance.

summon.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *somoundre*, from Old French *sumundre*, from Latin *summoneo*, itself from *sub* + *moneo*, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **monéyeti*, causative from **men-* (“to think”).

senses.definition: A form of selection bias in which only the people or things that "survived" some process are considered, while those that did not are inadvertently overlooked because of their lack of visibility.

core.definition: A mistake in reasoning that focuses only on the things that made it through a process, ignoring those that failed and are no longer visible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the VIE syllable in survivorship and the BY syllable in bias. The -ship ending is short and unstressed, and bias is two syllables, so say BY-us, not BY-ass.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term that names a reasoning error and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use survivorship bias in data science, finance, business writing, and everyday discussions of success stories. The phrase is common in analytics and statistics classes, and people often explain it with examples like wartime bombers or famous dropouts. It is precise and professional, so it fits meetings and academic writing better than casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Selection bias is the broader category of sampling errors. Survivorship bias is a specific case in which only the survivors of a process are included in the data.
Sampling bias refers to any unrepresentative sample. Survivorship bias is more specific and arises because failed cases are invisible.
Confirmation bias is seeking evidence that supports one's beliefs. Survivorship bias is missing data that failed to survive the process.

examples.everyday: When my friend says everyone who starts a business gets rich, that is survivorship bias, because we only hear about the winners.
examples.professional: Before we report the average customer lifetime value, we need to check for survivorship bias, since churned users are dropped from the dataset.
examples.analytical: Wald's study of returning bombers shows how survivorship bias can lead analysts to reinforce the very areas that need protection.

nuance.analogy: Survivorship bias is like judging a race only by the runners who finished, forgetting that many others dropped out along the way.
nuance.etymology: Survivorship comes from survive plus -ship; bias comes from French biais, 'slant', via Old Italian bieco.
common_mistakes: Saying the phrase with the wrong stress, such as sur-VIE-vur-SHIP.
Using survivorship bias for any kind of mistake, when it refers specifically to ignoring failed cases that are no longer visible.

senses.definition: To grab or bat quickly.
senses.example: The cat swiped at the shoelace.

senses.definition: To strike with a strong blow in a sweeping motion.
To scan or register by sliding (a swipecard etc.) through a reader.
senses.example: He swiped his card at the door.

senses.definition: To interact with a touch screen by drawing one's finger rapidly across it.
senses.example: Swipe left to hide the toolbar.

senses.definition: To swipe right on (someone) on a dating application.
To steal or snatch.
senses.example: Hey! Who swiped my lunch?

senses.definition: A quick grab, bat, or other motion with the hand or paw; a sweep.
A strong blow given with a sweeping motion, as with a bat or club.
An act of interacting with a touch screen by drawing the finger rapidly across it.
An act of passing a swipecard through a card reader.
A rough guess; an estimate or swag.
senses.example: Take a swipe at the answer, even if you're not sure.

senses.definition: An attack, insult or critical remark.
senses.example: The politician took a swipe at his opponents.

senses.definition: Poor, weak beer or other inferior alcoholic beverage; rotgut.
An instance of swiping, a kind of ellipsis. See swiping.

core.definition: To pass a card through a reader, or to slide a finger across a touchscreen to make something happen.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable: 'swipe' rhymes with 'ripe' and 'pipe.' Don't add a vowel between the w and the p, and keep the final p unreleased in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a routine, practical action in shops and on phones.
nuance.usage_note: In American stores, you'll hear 'Swipe your card' or 'Please swipe or insert your card.' Cashiers and card machines use the word constantly. In casual speech 'swipe' can also mean to grab something quickly or steal it, so context matters.

distinctions.note: 'Tap' means a quick touch; 'swipe' means a sliding motion across a surface.
'Insert' means putting a chip card into a slot, while 'swipe' means sliding a magnetic stripe card through a reader.

examples.everyday: Just swipe your card at the reader and then enter your PIN.
examples.professional: Employees swipe their badges at the side door, and the access log feeds our attendance dashboard.
examples.analytical: Every card swipe generates a timestamped record, which makes the temporal patterns in the dataset possible to model.

nuance.analogy: Like sliding a key through a lock in one smooth motion, not pushing it in.
nuance.etymology: Probably from an earlier sense of 'swipe' meaning a sweeping blow, possibly imitative.
common_mistakes: Saying 'swipe the card' with the wrong sense; in US stores, say 'swipe your card' or 'run your card.'
Confusing 'swipe' with 'insert,' which is used for chip cards.

swipe.etymology: From earlier *swip*, from Middle English *swippen*, *swype* (“to move violently”), from Old English *sweopian*, *swipian*, *swippan* (“to scourge, strike, beat, lash”), from **swippjan*, **swipōn*, **swipēn*, from Proto-Germanic **swipōną*, **swipjaną*,…

conversation.text: Go ahead and swipe your card whenever you're ready.
The machine wouldn't read my chip, so the cashier told me to swipe.
I swiped my card twice by accident. Will I be charged twice?

senses.definition: Representation of a concept through symbols or underlying meanings of objects or qualities.

An art movement originating in late 19th-century France and Belgium, seeking to represent absolute truths symbolically through language and metaphorical images, mainly as a reaction against naturalism and realism.

core.definition: The use of symbols to represent ideas or qualities, especially in art, literature and religion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'SIM'. The final syllable is a weak 'um', and the 'z' sounds like 'z' in 'lizard'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard term in literary analysis and sometimes in religion or politics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in English class, art and religious discussion, often as 'the symbolism in the novel' or 'religious symbolism.' It can sound academic in casual talk, so people might say 'symbols' or 'what it stands for' instead. In art history, it also refers to the late 19th-century Symbolist movement.

distinctions.note: A symbol is a single object or mark; symbolism is the broader system or practice of using symbols.
Allegory is an extended story in which every element stands for something; symbolism is usually more open and flexible.

examples.everyday: The movie has a lot of symbolism, like the red door that keeps coming back, so I had to think about it afterward.
examples.professional: The brand's symbolism of growth, with its rising arrows and green palette, supports the new campaign.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that the white whale's symbolism shifts across the novel, resisting any single reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a flag, where a bit of cloth carries a whole nation's history and values.
nuance.etymology: From the Greek sumbolon 'token, sign', with the suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Using 'symbolism' to mean any sign; it refers to the practice or system of symbols.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'sim-BOL-ism'; the main stress is on 'SIM'.

senses.definition: A brief summary of the major points of a written work, either as prose or as a table; an abridgment or condensation of a work.
A reference work containing brief articles that taken together give an overview of an entire field.
A prayer book for use by the laity of the church.

core.definition: A short summary of the main points of a book, movie, report, or other work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAP. The 'y' sound in the Greek root is spelled with p, so the middle is 'nap-sis', not 'sin-OP-sis'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds professional and efficient, and it is common in publishing, film, and business.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use synopsis for a short summary, especially of a movie, novel, or proposal. In everyday talk people say 'summary' or 'plot summary' more often. In film and publishing, a synopsis is usually a one- or two-page summary of the story.

distinctions.note: Summary is the everyday word for a short restatement; synopsis often suggests a more structured, formal summary of a whole work.
An abstract is a short summary placed at the start of an academic paper; a synopsis summarizes an entire work, often a story or proposal.

examples.everyday: Can you give me a quick synopsis of the movie before we start watching it?
examples.professional: Please send me a one-page synopsis of the proposal before Thursday's review.
examples.analytical: The author's synopsis of the argument omits the counterexample that drives the whole second chapter.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie trailer for a book: it shows the main shape of the story in a few minutes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synopsis, a seeing together or general view, from syn- 'together' and opsis 'sight'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as sin-OP-sis, with the stress on the first syllable.
Using the plural synopsises; the plural is synopses, pronounced sih-NAP-seez.

synopsis.etymology: From Late Latin *synopsis*, itself from Ancient Greek *σύνοψις*, from *σύν* (“with or whole”) + *ὄψις* (“view”) meaning whole view.

senses.definition: Someone who sells products or services by making unsolicited telephone calls.

core.definition: A person who sells products or services by calling people on the phone without their request.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress is on 'MAR', with a secondary stress on 'tel'. The final syllable is a reduced American 'er' and the middle 't' is a quick flap.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Many Americans find unsolicited sales calls annoying, so the word often carries irritation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use telemarketer for people who make sales calls, and the word often comes up when complaining about unwanted calls. A common reply to a cold call is 'Please take me off your list' or 'I'm not interested, thanks.' The word is neutral when used for a job, but it is usually said with an edge when discussing calls at dinner.

distinctions.note: Salesperson is general and can be in a store or on the phone; telemarketer specifically means someone who sells by phone.
A robocall is an automated recorded message; a telemarketer is a live person making the call.

examples.everyday: A telemarketer called during dinner again, so I just hung up.
examples.professional: Our sales team uses a telemarketer contractor to qualify leads before they reach account executives.
examples.analytical: The telemarketer's script relies on rapport built in the first ten seconds, which is why the sale often fails once the listener notices the pattern.

nuance.analogy: A telemarketer is like a door-to-door salesperson who only knocks on your phone.
nuance.etymology: From tele-, 'at a distance', from Greek tēle, plus marketer, from market.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in tel-uh-mar-KET-er.
Confusing telemarketer with telephone operator, which means a different job.

conversation.text: A telemarketer called during dinner again.
I told the telemarketer to take me off their list.
Put your number on the Do Not Call list to stop telemarketers.

core.definition: In the Bible, Teman is a grandson of Esau and a clan chief in Edom, and also the name of a region in Edom known for wisdom. It appears in Genesis 36:11 and Jeremiah 49:7.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so the name sounds like TEM-uhn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name and place with no everyday emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Teman in Bible study, sermons, and academic discussions of Edom. In casual conversation, people rarely mention it. Context usually makes clear whether it refers to a person or a region.

distinctions.note: Teman is a grandson of Esau and a region in Edom, while Tema is a son of Ishmael and a place in Arabia.
Teman is the name of the person or region, while Temanite is the adjective or the name for someone from Teman.

examples.everyday: My friend said she was reading about Teman in the book of Jeremiah and asked me what it meant.
examples.professional: When I taught the Edom oracles, I explained that Teman was both a clan name and a region associated with wisdom.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah 49:7 asks whether wisdom is no more in Teman, which implies that Teman had a reputation for wise counsel in the prophetic imagination.

common_mistakes: Confusing Teman with Tema.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Teman is a grandson of Esau named in Genesis 36:11, and the name later designates a region in Edom. Jeremiah 49:7 in the RSV asks whether wisdom is no more in Teman, linking the region with counsel and understanding. Amos 1:12 in the RSV announces fire on Teman, connecting it with judgment against Edom. Habakkuk 3:3 in the RSV says God came from Teman, which shows the region's place in Israel's religious imagination.

senses.definition: Something is more fun with more people.
A greater amount of something is better.
Used to welcome another person into a group activity or encourage them to join in, suggesting that they will be easily accommodated.

core.definition: A saying that more people make an activity more enjoyable, and that you are welcome to join in.

pronunciation.tip: The 'more' is pronounced with an r, and the final 'er' in 'merrier' is reduced to a soft, unstressed syllable. Stress 'mer' and keep the middle 'ee' short.

nuance.connotation: positive, friendly, and welcoming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to invite someone to join a party, dinner, or outing, often casually and warmly. It is common in everyday talk and sounds natural to friends, neighbors, and coworkers. A natural reply is 'Great, I'll bring a friend,' or 'Thanks, I'd love to come.'
